exercises.prompt: Which set names the three cardinal values?

choices.text: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem
Faith, sacrifice, and obedience
A passing mood, a crowd's taste, and a revealed order
Rationality, productiveness, and pride, taken as values rather than virtues

feedback.note: The cardinal values are reason, purpose, and self-esteem, because those are the primary values a rational life depends on. Faith, sacrifice, and obedience are substitutes from another code. A mood, a vote, and a revelation are not values one earns by thinking. Rationality, productiveness, and pride are the virtues that correspond to the three values, not a rival list of values.

exercises.prompt: What does cardinal mean when it is applied to these three values?

choices.text: A minor taste one may drop without affecting one's life
A rank conferred by an institution
Primary: a value one's own life as a rational being depends on
Whatever three things a person happens to like this week

feedback.note: Cardinal means primary, because these values are means to, and part of the realization of, one's ultimate value, one's own life. A minor taste can change without rewriting that life. An institutional rank and a weekly list of likes both miss the dependence: drop reason, purpose, or self-esteem, and a rational life does not remain intact.

exercises.prompt: Match each cardinal value to the role that makes it primary.

pairs.left: Reason
pairs.right: The value of knowing reality and guiding action by that knowledge

pairs.left: Purpose
pairs.right: The value of a chosen central goal that ranks one's other values

pairs.left: Self-esteem
pairs.right: The value of an earned conviction that one is competent and worthy

feedback.note: The three roles are distinct, because knowing, choosing a central goal, and holding an earned estimate of oneself are not the same act. They are cardinal together because a rational life needs all three. A mood cannot fill reason's role, an imposed mission cannot fill purpose's, and unearned flattery cannot fill self-esteem's.

exercises.prompt: Complete the set of the three cardinal values.

parts.text: The three cardinal values are reason, purpose, and

feedback.note: Self-esteem completes the set, because the cardinal values are reason, purpose, and the earned conviction that one is competent to think and worthy of living. Faith and sacrifice belong to a different morality. Applause is other people's noise, not a primary value one's life as a rational being depends on.

exercises.prompt: Why are these three cardinal, rather than a pile of things one happens to like?

choices.text: Because a short list is easier to memorize, and nothing further is at stake
Because one's life as a rational being depends on them, as means and as realization
Because a tradition named three, and the count is what makes them cardinal
Because any intense wish is cardinal if it is repeated three times

feedback.note: They are cardinal because a rational life depends on them: reason to know, purpose to integrate action, and self-esteem as the earned estimate of the person who does both. Memorizing a short list, inheriting a count, or repeating a wish does not make a value primary. A like that one's life does not require is not cardinal.

exercises.prompt: A speaker lists "wealth, fame, and power" as the three cardinal values. What has he missed?

choices.text: Nothing, if the three are strongly desired
That cardinal values must be impossible to achieve
That a cardinal value has to be a sacrifice
That the primary values are reason, purpose, and self-esteem, not rewards cut off from them

feedback.note: Wealth, fame, and power are not the cardinal set, because they do not name the values a rational life depends on as its means and realization. They can be results or even lesser values, but cut off from reason, purpose, and self-esteem they are a pile of likes. Desire does not promote them, and impossibility or sacrifice would not make a value cardinal.

exercises.prompt: Someone treats self-esteem as a gift from an audience and purpose as a mission he did not choose. Which values has he actually dropped?

choices.text: Purpose and self-esteem, while keeping the words
Neither, because an audience can choose his central goal for him
Reason only, because purpose need not be his and esteem need not be earned
All three, because reason forbids having any goal

feedback.note: A purpose is a goal one chooses, and self-esteem is earned, so an imposed mission and an audience's gift keep the names and drop the values. Reason does not forbid goals. It is what a real purpose has to answer to. The error is substitution, because the two values cannot be outsourced.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement of the three cardinal values.

feedback.note: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem are the cardinal values. Optional tastes are not primary, because a life as a rational being does not depend on every like. The corresponding virtues are rationality, productiveness, and pride, and they are virtues, not a second name for the values. Swapping the two lists collapses a value into the policy by which one achieves it.

exercises.prompt: Why is reason a value, and not only a name for a faculty one may ignore?

choices.text: Because a faculty is valuable only when it is left unused
Because knowledge and chosen action depend on it, so one must act to gain and keep it
Because a feeling becomes true when it is called reason
Because a vote can replace it whenever the vote is large

feedback.note: Reason is a cardinal value because one's life depends on knowing the facts and choosing by them. A faculty one ignores is not being gained or kept. A feeling does not become knowledge by a change of name, and a vote does not become perception. The value is the use of the faculty, not a label for abandoning it.

exercises.prompt: An engineer changes a design when a measurement contradicts it. Which value is he acting to keep?

choices.text: Reason, because he lets the facts decide and revises the conclusion
A whim, because changing one's mind is always a mood
A revealed order, because the measurement issued a command
None, because practical work is outside the cardinal values

feedback.note: He is keeping reason, because reason identifies the facts and he treats the measurement as decisive. Revising a conclusion is not a whim when the facts require it. A measurement is not a mystical command. Practical work is not outside the value. It is one of the places the value has to govern.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to what it does with reason.

pairs.left: Revise a claim the facts have refuted
Keep a wish after the facts refute it
Treat a feeling as proof
pairs.right: Puts a non-cognitive substitute in reason's place

feedback.note: Keeping reason means letting identification decide, including when a conclusion has to change. Holding a refuted wish refuses that value, because the wish is being protected from reality. A feeling is not a tool of knowledge, so treating it as proof replaces reason rather than using it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the office reason holds among the cardinal values.

parts.text: Reason is first because purpose and self-esteem depend on

feedback.note: Knowledge is what they depend on, because a purpose has to fit the facts and self-esteem has to be the estimate of a mind that actually thinks. Applause, revelation, and chance do not identify reality. Without knowledge, the other two cardinal values have nothing rational to rest on.

exercises.prompt: A planner says, "The feeling is strong, so it outranks the facts." What has he done to reason?

choices.text: He has used reason as his only judge of the value
He has kept reason first and used feeling only as a report of a prior judgment
He has shown that facts are created by intensity
He has replaced reason with a feeling and dropped the cardinal value

feedback.note: A feeling can report an estimate one already holds. It does not outrank the facts, and it does not identify them. Treating intensity as the judge replaces reason, which is the value this choice was supposed to keep. The facts are not created by how strong the feeling is.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the faculty one holds as a cardinal value?
exercises.quote: Reason is the faculty that identifies and integrates the material provided by man's senses.

choices.text: Reason invents reality out of feelings
Reason is a vote about what one wishes were true
Reason identifies and integrates what the senses provide
Reason is unnecessary once a purpose has been announced

feedback.quote: Reason is the faculty that identifies and integrates the material provided by man's senses.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 20
feedback.note: The passage establishes that reason identifies and integrates the material the senses provide. That is why it is a cardinal value: knowledge and chosen action depend on that work, and they do not depend on invention or on a vote. A purpose announced against the facts is not a substitute, because a purpose still has to be known before it can be chosen.

exercises.prompt: Why does reason come before purpose and self-esteem, rather than beside them as an optional extra?

choices.text: Because a purpose is rational even when it contradicts the facts
Because a rational purpose must fit reality, and self-esteem must estimate a mind that thinks
Because self-esteem invents the facts that purpose then cancels
Because the order is a custom with no dependence among the three

feedback.note: Reason is first because the other two depend on it. A purpose that contradicts the facts is a wish, not a rational purpose, and self-esteem that ignores whether one thinks is unearned. There is a real dependence here, not a custom. Self-esteem does not invent the facts, and a purpose does not cancel the need to know them.

exercises.prompt: What does rejecting reason amount to, once it is admitted as a cardinal value?

choices.text: Acting with no regard for the facts, or against them, while still having to live
A sharper kind of sight that no longer needs evidence
A way to make reality match a wish
A proof that purpose can be chosen with no knowledge

feedback.note: Rejecting reason does not sharpen sight or bend reality, because reason is the faculty that identifies the facts. What remains is action with no regard for those facts, by a being who still has to live. A purpose cannot be rationally chosen in that condition. The rejection does not free the other cardinal values. It undercuts them.

exercises.prompt: What is purpose, as one of the three cardinal values?

choices.text: A mood that expires when a stronger mood arrives
A mission imposed by a crowd, a fate, or a revelation
A chosen central goal that ranks a person's other values
The absence of any long-range goal, called freedom

feedback.note: Purpose is a chosen central goal, because a being who must choose needs a goal that ranks his other values into a life. A mood does not rank anything once it passes. An imposed mission was not chosen. Drifting is the lack of a purpose, not a purpose under a softer name.

exercises.prompt: Who selects a rational person's central purpose?

choices.text: He does, and the goal has to be one he can defend by the facts
A crowd, because purpose is an office other people fill
Nobody, because purposes are discovered as unchosen fate
A feeling, because intensity is the same fact as a long-range goal

feedback.note: A purpose is chosen by the person whose life it organizes, because a goal assigned by others is not his central value. It still has to fit the facts, or it is only a wish. Fate and intensity do not do the choosing. Applause can pressure him, but pressure is not a purpose he has selected.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to what it is, or is not.

pairs.left: Productive work chosen as the goal that ranks the rest
This hour's mood, to be replaced tonight
A life with no central goal
A mission one never judged and only obeys
pairs.right: An imposed substitute, not one's own purpose

feedback.note: A central purpose is a goal one chose and can stand behind, and for a rational life that goal is productive work. A rotating mood never settles into a purpose, because it does not rank a life. Drifting leaves the choice unmade. An imposed mission skips the choosing. None of the substitutes can do what a purpose does.

exercises.prompt: Complete the central purpose of a rational life, under one's own life as the ultimate value.

parts.text: That central purpose is productive

feedback.note: Productive work is the central purpose, because it is the chosen goal that can integrate a rational life in service of one's own life. Drift is the absence of a goal. Applause and sacrifice do not name the purpose. They are substitutes that would rank one's values by other people or by surrender, not by the work a life requires.

exercises.prompt: A goal contradicts the facts, and the person keeps it because the wish is intense. Is it a rational purpose?

choices.text: Yes, because intensity is the test of a purpose
Yes, because a purpose need not be judged by reason
Yes, if he calls the contradiction a higher kind of goal
No. A rational purpose has to fit reality. This one is a wish

feedback.note: Purpose depends on reason, because a goal that contradicts the facts cannot direct a life. Intensity does not convert the contradiction into a purpose. Calling it higher only renames a wish. The cardinal value is a chosen goal one can defend by the facts, not a feeling protected from them.

exercises.prompt: What does a purpose do to a person's other values?

choices.text: It erases them, so only one action remains possible
It ranks them, so lesser values are pursued in light of the central goal
It freezes them, so no new evidence may ever reorder a means
It cancels the need to choose, because the ranking happens automatically

feedback.note: A purpose ranks other values. It does not wipe them out, because a life still contains lesser goals that have to be ordered rather than denied. It does not freeze the means against new evidence, and it does not make the ranking automatic. The person still chooses, with the central goal as the measure of the rest.

exercises.prompt: Someone calls consumption without production his central purpose, and calls the work other people do a debt they owe him. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, because any intense aim is a rational purpose
The error is wanting one's own life as the ultimate value
A rational purpose is productive work in service of one's own life, not a claim on others' product
The error is having any long-range goal at all

feedback.note: The central purpose of a rational life is productive work, because that is how one's mind sustains one's life. Consumption without production, charged to other people, is not that goal. It is a wish to live by values one does not create. One's own life remains the ultimate value. A long-range goal is not the error. This goal is.

exercises.prompt: Build the account of purpose as a cardinal value.

feedback.note: Purpose is a chosen goal that ranks one's other values. An imposed fate was not chosen, and this hour's mood does not rank a life, because it expires when the feeling changes. The cardinal value requires a central goal the person selects and can defend by the facts, under his own life as the ultimate value.

exercises.prompt: What is self-esteem, as a cardinal value?

choices.text: The earned conviction that one is competent to think and worthy of living
A mood bestowed by whoever is watching
The belief that one should regard oneself as unworthy
Fame, accepted as proof that one need not think

feedback.note: Self-esteem is earned, and it has two parts: competence to think, and worthiness to live. An audience cannot bestow it, because the conviction is about one's own mind and one's own life. The duty to feel unworthy is the opposite conviction. Fame does not stand in for thinking, so it does not earn either part.

exercises.prompt: A woman thinks carefully and achieves her work, yet holds that she has no right to live. What is missing?

choices.text: Nothing, because competence alone is the whole of self-esteem
A larger audience
The conviction that she is worthy of living, which competence does not replace
A decision to stop thinking, so the conviction will feel humble

feedback.note: Self-esteem requires both parts, because the value is that one is able to think and worthy of the life that thinking makes possible. Competence without the right to live is only half. An audience cannot supply the missing half, and refusing to think would throw away the half she has. Humility of that kind is a rejection of the value, not a way of earning it.

exercises.prompt: Match each estimate to the value it does or does not name.

pairs.left: I can think, and I am worthy of my life, because I have earned both
I feel important when I am praised, and I do not ask whether I think
I should regard myself as unworthy, whatever I achieve

feedback.note: Self-esteem is an earned conviction of competence and worth. Praise without the question of whether one thinks is a borrowed mood, not that conviction. A standing verdict of unworthiness denies the value, because it treats the self as something one must not regard as worthy of living. Achievement does not obligate that verdict.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two parts of the value called self-esteem.

parts.text: Self-esteem is the earned conviction that one is
to think and
of living.

feedback.note: Competent and worthy are the two parts, because self-esteem estimates a mind that can think and a person who has a right to live. Fame and excuses do not fill either blank. They are substitutes: one is other people's attention, and the other is a pardon for not earning the conviction. Swapping the two parts does not state the value.

exercises.prompt: A man repeats "I am worthy" every morning and refuses to judge his actual thinking. Has he earned self-esteem?

choices.text: Yes, because a repeated sentence is the earning
Yes, if the sentence is said with intensity
Yes, because self-esteem is a gift one owes oneself without evidence
No. The conviction has to be earned by thinking and by achieving one's values

feedback.note: An unearned affirmation is not self-esteem, because the value is a conviction based on the competence one has actually practiced. Intensity does not supply the missing evidence. Calling it a gift severs it from earning. He has kept a sentence and dropped the cardinal value, which has to be gained and kept by the work of his mind.

exercises.prompt: Friends tell a person he may not respect himself until they grant permission. What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error, because self-esteem is an audience's permit
Self-esteem is earned by one's own thought and action, not issued by other people
The error is allowing him to think at all
The error is the idea that worthiness has anything to do with living

feedback.note: Other people do not issue self-esteem, because it is a conviction about one's own mind and one's own right to live. Permission would make it a grant, and a grant is not earned. Thinking is not the error. It is the competence the value names. Worthiness of living is the second part, not an optional extra.

exercises.prompt: A doctrine says the moral person cultivates the sense that he is unworthy of living. What does that doctrine attack?

choices.text: Self-esteem, by making unworthiness a duty rather than a conclusion one must earn past
Nothing, because unworthiness is the same conviction as competence
Only fame, which is the same thing as self-esteem
Reason, by requiring a person to think more carefully

feedback.note: The doctrine attacks self-esteem, because it demands the conviction that one is not worthy of living. That is not competence, and it is not a conclusion earned by thinking. It is a duty to hold oneself as low. Fame is not the value under attack. The doctrine does not ask for better thinking. It asks for a standing verdict against the self.

exercises.prompt: A person claims self-esteem while boasting that he never bothers to think. What is the claim?

choices.text: The full cardinal value, because worthiness does not require a mind
Reason, practiced in a quicker form
A pretense. Competence to think is half of self-esteem, and he has refused it
Purpose, because refusing to think is a central goal

feedback.note: Self-esteem includes the conviction that one is competent to think, so a boast of not thinking contradicts the value. Worthiness does not survive that refusal, because the life one would be worthy of is a rational life. The claim is not reason in disguise, and it is not a purpose. It is an unearned estimate standing in for the cardinal value.

exercises.prompt: How do reason, purpose, and self-esteem stand to one another?

choices.text: Each can replace the other two, so any one is enough
Each depends on the other two, and together they serve one's own life
They are three tastes that need not be acted on
Self-esteem invents the facts, and purpose cancels the need to think

feedback.note: They are one set because each depends on the other two. Reason makes a rational purpose possible, achieving that purpose supports self-esteem, and self-esteem is the conviction that one can think and is worthy of the life one is shaping. Any single item, cut off from the others, is no longer the cardinal value it was. A taste one need not act on is not this set.

exercises.prompt: A researcher knows a great deal and refuses every central goal. What is missing from the set?

choices.text: Purpose, so the knowledge is not integrated into a life he is choosing
Nothing, because reason alone is the whole set
Self-esteem, which requires him to stop knowing things
A revealed mission to replace the choosing

feedback.note: Knowledge without a central goal is reason with purpose dropped, because the values do not form a hierarchy he can live by. Reason is not the whole set. Self-esteem is not earned by refusing to know. A revealed mission would not restore his purpose. It would replace the choice the cardinal value requires.

exercises.prompt: Match each break in the set to the result.

pairs.left: A goal held against the facts
pairs.right: Purpose without reason, which is a wish

pairs.left: An estimate of oneself with no thinking and no achieved goal
Knowledge with no central goal
Thinking, a chosen productive goal, and an earned conviction of worth

feedback.note: Reason without purpose leaves knowledge unintegrated. Purpose without reason is a wish, because it does not fit the facts. Self-esteem without the other two is a pretense, not the earned conviction. Held together, the three are the means to and the realization of one's own life. None of the breaks is a harmless omission.

exercises.prompt: Complete the virtues that correspond to the three cardinal values.

parts.text: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem correspond to rationality, productiveness, and

feedback.note: Pride corresponds to self-esteem, because it is the moral ambition by which one earns the conviction of competence and worth. Rationality and productiveness are the other two corresponding virtues, already named. Mercy, faith, and obedience are not members of this set, and adding them would invent a virtue the three values do not require.

exercises.prompt: Which list names virtues corresponding to the cardinal values, rather than the values themselves?

choices.text: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem
Faith, sacrifice, and a public mood
Whim, drift, and unearned praise
Rationality, productiveness, and pride

feedback.note: Rationality, productiveness, and pride are the virtues by which one gains and keeps reason, purpose, and self-esteem. The first list names the values, not the virtues, because a value is not the policy that achieves it. Faith, sacrifice, and a mood belong to another code. Whim, drift, and unearned praise do not achieve the set.

exercises.prompt: A man says he values reason, but he will not practice rationality when a fact is inconvenient. What has come apart?

choices.text: Nothing, because a value does not have to be acted on
Pride and productiveness only, which have no link to reason
The value and the virtue. Keeping reason means practicing rationality
Self-esteem, which consists in refusing inconvenient facts

feedback.note: A value one will not act to keep is not being held, because the cardinal values are values one gains and keeps by the corresponding virtues. Rationality is that virtue for reason. Refusing an inconvenient fact drops both. Self-esteem does not consist in that refusal. It estimates a mind that faces the facts. The other virtues are linked to reason as well, since rationality is primary, but the break he named is this one.

exercises.prompt: Someone claims self-esteem, has no purpose, and treats reason as optional. Which description fits?

choices.text: The set, because self-esteem can invent the other two
A pretense of self-esteem, with purpose and reason both missing
A rational purpose, because optional reason is still reason
Pride, which requires that one not think and not choose a goal

feedback.note: Self-esteem without reason and purpose is not the cardinal value, because there is nothing earned to estimate: no thinking, and no central goal achieved. It cannot invent the other two. Optional reason is reason dropped, not a purpose. Pride is the virtue of earning one's worth, not a license to skip the thinking and the goal.

exercises.prompt: Build the dependence among the three cardinal values.

feedback.note: Reason makes a rational purpose possible, and achieving that purpose supports self-esteem. Applause does not bestow the third value, and purpose does not replace the need to think, because a wish against the facts is not a purpose. The three stand or fall together as the means to and the realization of one's own life.

exercises.prompt: Who properly gains by a person's own action, in a rational morality?

choices.text: He does, and the interest he acts on has to be one his life as a rational being requires
Someone else must gain, and he must lose
Whoever has the strongest need, regardless of his values
No one. A moral action is one from which nobody gains

feedback.note: The actor properly gains by his own action, because a rational morality holds that he must act for his own self-interest, and that interest is what his life as a rational being requires. A duty to lose, a stranger's need taken as a claim, and a ban on anyone gaining all deny that the actor may be the one who benefits. They are altruism or a confusion with it, not this principle.

exercises.prompt: A carpenter builds a table, sells it, and keeps the payment because the work was his. What is the moral point of the payment?

choices.text: The payment is a confession that he should have given the table away
The payment is proper only if a stranger needed the money more
He is the one who properly gains by work he chose, through a value he created
The payment is a whim, so the sale has no moral description

feedback.note: He properly gains because the action was his, the table was a value he created, and the payment is what he receives for it. Giving it away as a duty would make someone else the one who gains by his work. A stranger's greater need is not the measure. The sale is not a whim. It is production followed by trade, which is how a rational interest is pursued.

exercises.prompt: Match each rule to the person it treats as the one who should gain.

pairs.left: Act for your own rational interest
Live so that others gain and you lose
Act so that nobody may benefit
pairs.right: No one, which is not a moral purpose

feedback.note: A rational morality names the actor as the one who properly gains, because the interest is his own life. The demand that he lose so others gain is the rejected code. A ban on anyone benefiting is not a loftier version of the same idea. It still denies that his action is for him, and it gives the action no life-serving purpose at all.

exercises.prompt: Complete the kind of interest the actor may pursue.

parts.text: The actor acts for his own
, not for a whim and not as a duty to lose.

feedback.note: Rational interest names the stake, because the interest has to be what his life as a rational being requires, not a passing urge and not a duty to come out behind. Whim, surrender, and debt are the errors: one is subjectivism, and the other two hand the gain to someone else or to no purpose he holds. The actor remains the one who properly benefits.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the person who acts and the interest he acts on?
exercises.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds that the actor must always be the beneficiary of his action and that man must act for his own rational self-interest.

choices.text: The actor must lose, and a stranger's need selects the interest
The actor must be the one who gains, and the interest must be his rational interest
Any whim counts as the interest, including a plan to rob
The actor may gain only after he has sacrificed a higher value

feedback.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds that the actor must always be the beneficiary of his action and that man must act for his own rational self-interest.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introduction," The Virtue of Selfishness, ix
feedback.note: The passage establishes that the actor must be the one who gains by his action and that he must act for his own rational self-interest. A duty to lose contradicts it. A whim, and robbery in particular, is not a rational interest, because rational names what his life requires, not whatever he feels like seizing. A prior sacrifice is not the price of being allowed to gain.

exercises.prompt: A slogan says, "Count the action moral only when you come out worse." What is the slogan demanding?

choices.text: That the actor be the one who gains by his own rational action
That production and trade be the form of his interest
Nothing that touches who gains. It is advice about bookkeeping
That he not be the one who gains, which is the demand a rational morality rejects

feedback.note: The slogan demands that the actor lose, because "come out worse" means someone else, or no purpose of his, gets the gain. That is the demand rejected by the principle that he is the proper gainer by his own action. It is not bookkeeping advice. Production and trade are how he pursues a rational interest, and the slogan forbids the pursuit to succeed.

exercises.prompt: Why does "rational" restrict the interest, rather than leaving every urge eligible?

choices.text: Because an interest is what man's life requires, not a whim and not a license to rob
Because rational means whatever is intense, including a destructive urge
Because the actor may gain only from other people's losses
Because an interest is moral only when he is not the one who benefits

feedback.note: Rational restricts the interest because man's life, not a feeling, decides what is in his interest. A destructive urge and a plan to rob can feel like gains and still work against that life. Gaining from other people's losses, as a policy, is the robber's version, not the rational one. The restriction does not cancel his place as the one who properly benefits. It identifies which benefits count.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle about who an action is for.

feedback.note: The actor properly gains by his own action, in pursuit of his rational interest. A duty to lose hands the gain away, and any whim pretends that intensity is an interest, because an interest is fixed by what his life as a rational being requires. Robbery is not smuggled in under the principle. The gain has to be one that life permits him to seek.

exercises.prompt: What is the moral demand this account rejects?

choices.text: That a person may value the people he loves
That a person must live for others, as a duty, and must not live for his own sake
That a person may trade value for value
That kindness toward someone he values can be part of his own hierarchy

feedback.note: The rejected demand is that one must live for others as a moral duty, with no right to exist for one's own sake. Valuing people one loves, trading, and kindness inside one's own hierarchy are not that demand, because they do not make another person's need, as such, the purpose of one's life. The demand is altruism. The alternatives are ways of pursuing one's own values.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says your life is justified only by service, and any gain to you is a moral stain. Which demand is this?

choices.text: The demand that you live for others and treat your own benefit as a fault
The claim that you are the proper gainer by your own rational action
A permission to value a friend because the friend is a value to you
A reminder that production and robbery are different

feedback.note: Service as the only justification, and your gain as a stain, is the demand to live for others, because it denies that you may exist for your own sake. It is not the principle that you properly gain by your own action. Valuing a friend and distinguishing production from robbery are compatible with that principle. The speaker is not describing either of them.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement to the demand it does or does not make.

pairs.left: You must live for others as a duty
You may value a person who is a real value in your life
You must come out worse, or the action is stained

feedback.note: The duty to live for others and the stain on your own gain are one demand, because both deny that your life is an end. Valuing a person who is a value to you does not make that person a duty and does not require you to lose. The rewording about a stain is not a milder version. It is the same rejection of your place as the one who properly gains.

as a moral duty.

feedback.note: Others completes the rejected demand, because the duty is to take other people as the purpose of one's life. Oneself is the purpose a rational morality accepts. Reality and production are not the names of that duty. They are what a person who lives for his own sake has to face and to do. The blank is the beneficiary the altruist demand appoints.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about whether the good requires sacrifice?
exercises.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds that human good does not require human sacrifices and cannot be achieved by the sacrifice of anyone to anyone.

choices.text: The good requires each person to live as a victim for others
The good is achieved by sacrificing others to oneself
Sacrifices are the only means to a human good
The good does not require human sacrifices, and it cannot be achieved by sacrificing anyone to anyone

feedback.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds that human good does not require human sacrifices and cannot be achieved by the sacrifice of anyone to anyone.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 31
feedback.note: The passage establishes that human good does not require sacrifices and cannot be achieved by sacrificing anyone to anyone. A duty to live as a victim contradicts it, and so does a permission to sacrifice other people, because both are sacrifices of someone to someone. The good is not reached by that means. The rejected demand to live for others depends on the means the passage rules out.

exercises.prompt: Why is "live for others" not the same claim as "other people can be values to you"?

choices.text: They are the same claim, because any concern for a person is a duty to live for strangers
They differ only in tone, and the duty is what both assert
A value is someone you gain from having in your life. A duty says their need outranks your life
A value requires you to lose. A duty allows you to gain

feedback.note: They differ because a person you value is part of your own hierarchy, and acting for that person can be acting for your own life. The duty says you must live for others whether or not they are values to you, and that your need to live is what must give way. The second is the rejected demand. The first is not a stain and not a sacrifice when the person outranks the alternative you give up.

exercises.prompt: A rule says you may seek your own good only by sacrificing other people to it. Does rejecting "live for others" license that rule?

choices.text: Yes, because the alternative to living for others is living off others
No. The good cannot be achieved by sacrificing anyone to anyone, including them to you
Yes, if the sacrifice is called rational interest
No, only because you are forbidden to gain at all

feedback.note: Rejecting the duty to live for others does not license sacrificing them, because the good cannot be achieved by the sacrifice of anyone to anyone. Calling the seizure a rational interest does not make it one. The alternative is not living off others. It is living by your own production and trade, as the one who gains by values you create. A ban on your gaining is the duty again, not the correction.

exercises.prompt: Build the demand that is rejected, so it stays distinct from valuing a person.

feedback.note: The rejected demand is that one must live for others as a moral duty. Valuing a friend is not that demand, and a license to sacrifice them is not the alternative, because the good requires no sacrifice of anyone to anyone. The duty makes other people the purpose of your life. A friend who is a value to you does not.

exercises.prompt: In this contrast, what does altruism hold?

choices.text: Others must be the ones who gain by your action, and self-sacrifice is the ideal
You must be the one who gains, by a rational interest
Kindness toward a person you value is the whole of the doctrine
Respect for other people's rights is the sacrificial ideal

feedback.note: Altruism holds that others must be the ones who gain by your action and that self-sacrifice is the moral ideal, because on that code your own benefit is what disqualifies an action. Kindness toward someone you value, and respect for rights, are not that doctrine. They do not say that another person's need, as such, is the justification of your life. The contrast is about who is allowed to gain.

exercises.prompt: By the altruist test as stated here, when is an action good, and when is it evil?

choices.text: Good when it sustains your life, evil when it destroys it
Good when you produce, evil when you rob
Good when both parties gain by trade, evil when one is forced
Good when others gain and you do not, evil when you are the one who gains

feedback.note: On this statement of altruism the only test is who gains, because an action for others is called good and an action for yourself is called evil. That is not the life standard, not the difference between production and robbery, and not the trader's test of mutual gain. Those three can all approve an action in which you benefit. Altruism, so stated, cannot.

exercises.prompt: Match each policy to the code that claims it.

pairs.left: Your need to live is not a justification. Service is
You are the proper gainer by your own rational action
Help a friend because that friend is a great value to you

feedback.note: Altruism makes service the justification of your existence and treats your own life as morally weightless. Rational self-interest says you properly gain by your action. Helping a friend because the friend is a value to you serves your hierarchy, so it is not the code that says others, as such, must be the ones who gain. The third policy can be selfish in the rational sense.

exercises.prompt: Complete what altruism treats as the ideal.

parts.text: Altruism treats self-sacrifice as the moral

feedback.note: Ideal is what altruism makes of self-sacrifice, because the doctrine holds that giving yourself up is the virtue, not a breach. Crime, error, and whim are judgments a life-based morality can pass on that surrender. They do not name the status altruism assigns it. The ideal is precisely what a rational code refuses to praise.

exercises.prompt: Why is generosity toward a person you value, inside your own hierarchy, not altruism?

choices.text: Because altruism is any action that benefits anyone, including you
Because generosity is moral only when you surrender a higher value from duty
Because you are achieving a value you hold, not living for others as a duty
Because a gift is altruism whenever the other person is pleased

feedback.note: The generosity is not altruism, because the person is a value in your hierarchy and the action serves your life rather than a duty to make others the point of it. Altruism is not "any benefit to anyone." It is the code that requires the benefit to be theirs and the loss to be yours, as a duty. Pleasure on their side does not by itself convert your choice into that code. Surrendering a higher value from duty would be the doctrine. This case is not that surrender.

exercises.prompt: A donor pays a stranger's project, not because the stranger is a value to him, but because he believes his own life is not a justification. Which code is he following?

choices.text: A rational interest, because the money left his hand
Altruism, because the duty to serve, and not his values, selected the action
Justice, because the stranger's need was a fact about desert
Trade, because the stranger received a value

feedback.note: He is following altruism, because the reason was that his own life does not justify his action, which is the demand to live for others. The money moving is not enough to make an interest rational. Need is not desert, so justice is not what he applied. The stranger's receipt is not a trade, because nothing was given in return and he did not judge the project as a value to himself. The selector was the duty.

exercises.prompt: Which error treats respect for other people's rights as if it were altruism?

choices.text: The error of equating "do not sacrifice them" with "live for them"
There is no error, because rights are a duty to serve
The error of distinguishing production from robbery
The error of allowing any person to be a value to another

feedback.note: Respecting rights means you do not seize their lives or their work, not that you live for them, because "do not sacrifice anyone to anyone" includes not sacrificing them to you and does not appoint you as their servant. Calling rights a duty to serve collapses that line into altruism. The production-robbery distinction and the permission to value people are not the error. They are parts of the rational alternative.

exercises.prompt: Build what altruism asks, as against a rational interest.

feedback.note: Altruism asks that others be the ones who gain and that self-sacrifice be the ideal. Keeping the gain is the rational alternative, and kindness inside your own values is not the doctrine, because that kindness does not require you to live for others as a duty. The code's test is who benefits. If the answer must be "not you," the code is altruism.

exercises.prompt: Two men end the week with money. One made goods and sold them. The other took a neighbor's goods. What is the moral difference?

choices.text: None, because both gained cash
Production creates a value. Robbery seizes a value someone else created
Robbery is the rational form, because the robber avoided effort
Production is the stain, because the producer gained

feedback.note: There is a moral difference because one man's interest took the form of production and the other's took the form of robbery. Cash does not erase it. Avoiding effort is not what makes an interest rational. The producer's gain is not a stain. He is the proper gainer by a value he created. The robber made a victim, which is sacrificing someone else to himself.

exercises.prompt: A critic calls both men selfish and stops there, as if the word ended the question. What has he refused to judge?

choices.text: Whether the interest was production or robbery, which is the moral difference
Whether both men breathed, which is the moral difference
Whether the producer failed to live for the robber
Nothing. Selfish names a single policy, and both men practiced it

feedback.note: He has refused the difference between seeking one's interest in production and seeking it in robbery, because those are not one policy. Breathing is not the difference. The producer does not owe the robber a life of service. Using one word for both is a package deal. It lets the robber borrow the name of a rational interest without the reality.

exercises.prompt: Match each action to the interest it actually pursues.

pairs.left: Make a value and trade it
Take a value someone else made
Call both by one name and stop
pairs.right: A refusal to judge the difference

feedback.note: Production is a way of acting for one's own life, because the actor creates the value he gains. Robbery is a way of sacrificing someone else to oneself, and the cash does not make it the same interest. Stopping at one label refuses the judgment. A rational morality does not license the seizure by allowing the actor to be the one who gains. The gain has to be of a kind his life, and theirs, can survive.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast the principle draws.

parts.text: There is a moral difference between seeking one's interest in production and seeking it in

feedback.note: Robbery completes the contrast, because that is the policy of seizing a value one did not create, and it is morally different from production. Trade, work, and thought belong on the production side, or on the means to it. They do not name the thing production is being distinguished from. The difference is the point a single smear-word is designed to hide.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about self-interest in production and self-interest in robbery?
exercises.quote: There is a fundamental moral difference between a man who sees his self-interest in production and a man who sees it in robbery.

choices.text: They are morally the same whenever both yield cash
Production is immoral because the producer is the one who gains
There is a fundamental moral difference between them
Robbery is moral if the robber describes it as need

feedback.quote: There is a fundamental moral difference between a man who sees his self-interest in production and a man who sees it in robbery.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introduction," The Virtue of Selfishness, ix
feedback.note: The passage establishes a fundamental moral difference between the man who sees his interest in production and the man who sees it in robbery. Equal cash does not cancel the difference, because one creates a value and the other seizes it. The producer's gain is not what makes him immoral. Need does not rename a seizure as production. The word interest does not do that work either.

exercises.prompt: A company builds tools and sells them to willing buyers. A gang steals the tools and sells them to the same buyers. A headline calls both "profit-seeking." What should be added?

choices.text: Nothing. The headline has finished the moral judgment
That the company failed unless the gang gained more
That the buyers' willingness makes the theft a trade
That one profit came from production and the other from robbery

feedback.note: The headline needs the difference, because profit from tools one made and sold is not profit from tools one stole. The buyers' willingness to purchase from the gang does not turn the theft into a trade with the company. The company does not owe the gang a larger gain. Stopping at "profit-seeking" repeats the package deal the moral difference exists to break.

exercises.prompt: Does "the actor properly gains" mean he may seize another person's product whenever the seizure benefits him?

choices.text: Yes, because a benefit is a rational interest by definition
No. A rational interest is not a license to rob, and the victim's loss is not his production
Yes, if he calls the victim's work a debt
No, because he is forbidden to benefit from anything

feedback.note: It does not license the seizure, because there is a moral difference between production and robbery, and a benefit got by robbery is not the rational interest of a being who lives by reason. Calling the victim's work a debt does not create the value. The alternative is not a ban on benefiting. It is benefiting by values one creates and trades, so that nobody is sacrificed to anybody.

exercises.prompt: Which action is the actor's rational gain, rather than a seizure?

choices.text: She writes a program, a client pays the price she asked, and both understand the exchange
He copies her program, sells it as his, and keeps the price
A board takes her payment because the members did not write anything this year
A stranger demands the program on the ground that she has no right to gain

feedback.note: The sale she chose is her rational gain, because she produced the value and the client paid for it. The copy sold as his work is robbery by fraud. The board's taking is a seizure of the unearned. The stranger's demand is the altruist claim that she must not be the one who gains. Only the first action is production. The others all treat her product as theirs to dispose of.

exercises.prompt: Which account is rational selfishness, once the wording is made precise?

choices.text: Concern with any urge, including an urge to rob or to destroy one's mind
A duty to live for others, under a friendlier name
Concern with one's own interests, as man's life requires, with oneself as the one who gains
A license to sacrifice other people whenever the sacrifice pays

feedback.note: Rational selfishness is concern with one's own interests as man's life requires, with oneself as the one who properly gains, because that is what the dictionary word means once a rational standard identifies the interests. An urge, a duty to live for others, and a license to sacrifice them are the three misreadings. They are whim-worship, altruism, and predation. None of them is the principle.

exercises.prompt: A friend is a great value in your life, and you pay for her care rather than buy a luxury you rank lower. A critic calls the payment altruism and a sacrifice. What is it?

choices.text: Neither. You are acting on your own hierarchy, and she outranks the luxury
Altruism, because she benefits
A sacrifice, because you did not buy the luxury
Robbery, because the physician was paid

feedback.note: It is neither altruism nor a sacrifice, because you gain a value you rank higher than the luxury, and you are not living for others as a duty. Her benefit does not convert the act into altruism. The unbought luxury is a lesser value given up, not a greater one surrendered. Paying the physician is trade, not robbery. The critic's labels ignore your hierarchy.

exercises.prompt: Match each slogan to the view it actually expresses.

pairs.left: I keep what I earn, and I live for my own sake
I take what they earn, and I call the taking my interest
I give up what I value most, because their need is my duty
I help the person I value, within the rank she has in my life
pairs.right: Not altruism and not a sacrifice

feedback.note: Keeping what one earns is concern with one's own life. Taking what others earn is robbery, even if it is called an interest, because the moral difference remains. Giving up a highest value from duty is altruism. Help that respects one's own hierarchy is a rational action for a value one holds. The four slogans are not synonyms. The wording is what makes them look alike.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the word "selfishness," and what must still be added?
exercises.quote: Yet the exact meaning and dictionary definition of the word "selfishness" is: concern with one's own interests.

choices.text: It means sacrificing others, and nothing further is required
It means concern with one's own interests, which a rational code then judges by man's life
It means living for others as a duty
It means acting on any whim, so production and robbery are the same

feedback.quote: Yet the exact meaning and dictionary definition of the word "selfishness" is: concern with one's own interests.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introduction," The Virtue of Selfishness, vii
feedback.note: The passage establishes the dictionary meaning: concern with one's own interests. It does not say that any whim is an interest, and it does not equate production with robbery, because a rational code still has to identify the interests by what man's life requires. Living for others is a different morality. Sacrificing others is predation. The definition alone is not yet the whole code, and it is not those errors either.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast the wording often hides.

parts.text: Kindness toward a person one values is not
when it serves one's own hierarchy.

feedback.note: Altruism is the hidden substitution, because kindness inside one's hierarchy serves a value one holds and is not a duty to live for others. Action, choice, and value are what the kindness is, so they do not name the error. Calling every benefit to another person altruism erases the difference between a value and a sacrificial duty.

exercises.prompt: A column calls a farmer selfish for selling his crop, and calls a looter selfish for burning it. Then it says the two facts are one vice. What has the column done?

choices.text: It has applied the difference between production and robbery
It has shown that selling is a duty to live for the looter
It has shown that the looter acted on a rational interest
It has used one word to erase a moral difference the word does not erase

feedback.note: The column has packaged two actions under one smear, because concern with one's own interests is not the same policy as destroying someone else's product. The farmer's sale is production and trade. The burning is predation. Neither the duty to live for the looter nor a rational interest in arson follows from the shared adjective. The wording changed. The actions did not become one action.

exercises.prompt: Which rewording still states a rational self-interest, rather than altruism or predation?

choices.text: "My interest is whatever I can seize, and their loss is the proof"
"My life is justified only if I come out worse than the people I serve"
"I act for my own life, by producing, and I do not sacrifice them or myself"
"A passing urge is my interest, and no further test is allowed"

feedback.note: The third wording keeps the actor as the one who gains, names production as the means, and refuses sacrifices in both directions, because that is rational self-interest. Seizure is predation. Coming out worse is altruism. An untested urge is a whim. Different sentences can state the same principle or smuggle in its opposites. The test is the content, not the presence of the word interest.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that survives a change of wording.

feedback.note: Rational selfishness is concern with one's own interests as man's life requires. A license to rob and a duty to lose are the two distortions, because one sacrifices others and the other sacrifices oneself. Kindness toward a person one values, inside one's hierarchy, fits the principle. It does not become altruism when the wording turns hostile, and it does not become a whim when the wording turns loose.

exercises.prompt: What kind of fact is happiness, as against a thing or a rule?

choices.text: A possession one can store, like cash in a drawer
A state of consciousness, the emotional form of a life that is going well
A moral rule that commands a feeling, whether or not any value was achieved
A mood one invents, with no connection to one's life

feedback.note: Happiness is a state of consciousness, because it is the emotional form of successful living, not an object one puts away. It is not a rule commanding a feeling in the absence of achieved values, and it is not a mood invented apart from one's life. Treating it as cash confuses a psychological state with a thing.

exercises.prompt: A man says he will "get some happiness" the way he picks up a package. What has he misunderstood?

choices.text: That happiness is a state of consciousness, not a detachable object
Nothing, because a state of consciousness can be shipped
That happiness is a rule he can obey without living
That a package is the standard of value

feedback.note: He has treated a state of consciousness as a package, because happiness is not detachable from the consciousness that has achieved its values. It cannot be shipped apart from the life. Calling it a rule one obeys without living makes the same cut. A package is not the standard of value, and that was not the confusion he needs corrected first.

exercises.prompt: Match each label to what it does, or does not, name.

pairs.left: A state of consciousness
A stored possession
A rule requiring a feeling no values support
A mood invented apart from one's life
pairs.right: An invented mood, not that state

feedback.note: Happiness is a state of consciousness, because it is how a successful life feels to the person living it. A stored object, a groundless rule, and an invented mood are the usual mislabelings. None of them is a state that proceeds from achieved values. The negative three fail for different reasons, and none of them is the emotional form of living well.

exercises.prompt: Complete the kind of thing happiness is.

parts.text: Happiness is a state of
, not a possession and not a groundless rule.

feedback.note: Consciousness names the kind of fact happiness is, because it is an emotional state of the person who has achieved his values. Cash, obedience, and noise are the wrong kind of thing: a possession, a command, and a sensation with no claim to be the state. None of them is how a successful life is experienced.

exercises.prompt: Can a person be ordered to feel happiness, as a duty, while renouncing every value he holds?

choices.text: Yes, because happiness is a rule and does not depend on values
Yes, if the order is loud enough to count as a possession
Yes, because renouncing values is how the state is produced
No. The state is not a command, and it does not arise from renouncing one's values

feedback.note: Happiness cannot be ordered into existence, because it is a state of consciousness that proceeds from achieved values, not a duty to feel. Renouncing one's values removes the achievement the state comes from. Volume does not turn an order into a possession of the feeling. The demand treats an effect as if it were a rule one could obey in the dark.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about what happiness is?
exercises.quote: Happiness is that state of consciousness which proceeds from the achievement of one's values.

choices.text: Happiness is a possession stored apart from any value
Happiness is a command to feel pleasure while renouncing one's values
Happiness is the state of consciousness that proceeds from achieving one's values
Happiness is a whim, and achieved values are irrelevant to it

feedback.quote: Happiness is that state of consciousness which proceeds from the achievement of one's values.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 123
feedback.note: The passage establishes that happiness is that state of consciousness which proceeds from the achievement of one's values. It is not an object, a command, or a whim, because the state depends on values actually achieved. A duty to feel pleasure while renouncing values contradicts the passage. So does any account that cuts the state off from the achievement.

exercises.prompt: A woman feels a brief glow and calls it happiness, though it clashes with every value she claims to hold. What is the glow?

choices.text: Happiness, because any glow is that state
Not happiness in this sense, because the state does not clash with one's values
The standard of value, because a glow outranks a life
Proof that values are achieved by being betrayed

feedback.note: A glow that clashes with her values is not the state that proceeds from achieving them, because happiness is non-contradictory in that sense: it does not come from betraying what one holds. Any pleasant moment is not automatically that state. The glow is not the standard of value. Man's life remains the standard, and a betrayal does not count as an achievement of one's values.

exercises.prompt: Build the identification of what happiness is.

feedback.note: Happiness is a state of consciousness, not a stored possession or a groundless rule. A whim is a further error, and so is treating the state as the standard of value, because the standard is man's life and the state is an effect of achieving one's values. The sentence keeps the kind of fact clear before the cause is applied to cases.

exercises.prompt: What does the state of happiness proceed from?

choices.text: The achievement of one's values
The renunciation of one's values
The mere wish to have a value, with no achievement
A clash between the feeling and every value one holds

feedback.note: Happiness proceeds from the achievement of one's values, because the state is the emotional consequence of having gained or kept them. Renouncing them removes the cause. A wish is not yet an achievement. A clash with one's values is the opposite of the non-contradictory joy the state names. The feeling does not come first and then create the values.

exercises.prompt: An architect names a building as his value and has not designed it, built it, or taken any step. Where is the happiness that would proceed from that value?

choices.text: Already his, because naming a value is achieving it
Impossible ever, because achievement destroys happiness
Not yet. The state follows the achievement, and the achievement has not happened
His if he renounces the building and feels relieved

feedback.note: Naming a value is not achieving it, so the state that proceeds from achievement has not arisen. Relief at renouncing the building would not be that state, because it comes from giving the value up rather than from realizing it. Achievement is the cause of this happiness, not its enemy. The order is the whole point.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the happiness it can or cannot yield.

pairs.left: A value one has actually achieved
pairs.right: The state that proceeds from that achievement

pairs.left: A value one has only wished for
A value one renounces in order to feel noble

feedback.note: Only the achieved value yields the state, because happiness proceeds from achievement and not from a wish or from a surrender. Renouncing a value in order to feel noble inverts the cause. The nobility is a claim that one's loss is a success, and that claim does not produce the state that follows from gaining what one values.

exercises.prompt: Complete the source from which that state proceeds.

parts.text: Happiness proceeds from the achievement of one's

feedback.note: Values completes the principle, because the state follows what one has actually gained or kept, not a whim, a surrender, or someone else's order. Whims and renunciations are the errors: one has no tie to an achieved value, and the other is the attempt to get the state by giving values up. An order cannot substitute for the achievement.

exercises.prompt: A fraud makes a man rich by faking his product. He says the money is an achieved value, so the glow is happiness. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, because cash obtained any way is an achieved value
The glow is happiness only if he also feels guilty
Faking reality is a way of achieving a value one's life can rely on
A value obtained by faking reality is not a value the state can proceed from

feedback.note: Happiness proceeds from the achievement of one's values, and the unreal is not such a value, because a fraud does not become real when it pays. Guilt is not what would convert the glow into happiness. The glow may be a feeling. It is not the state that proceeds from values one can actually live by. Faking is a breach of the values, not their achievement.

exercises.prompt: A moralist says one becomes happy by renouncing one's happiness and betraying one's values. What does that advice demand?

choices.text: The normal cause of the state, which is achievement
The state, while forbidding the achievement it proceeds from
A stricter attention to the values one is acting to keep
Nothing about happiness. It is advice about a possession

feedback.note: The advice demands the effect while forbidding the cause, because happiness proceeds from achieved values and the advice tells one to betray them. That is not a stricter loyalty to one's values. It is a negation of them. Happiness is not a possession one can collect while giving up the life that would have produced the state.

exercises.prompt: Two painters hold the same values. One has finished the work she judged worth doing. The other has announced the project and stopped. Who has the happiness that proceeds from those values?

choices.text: The one who finished, because the state follows achievement, not an announcement
Both, because holding a value and achieving it are the same event
The one who stopped, because renunciation is a higher achievement
Neither, because happiness is a rule unrelated to work

feedback.note: The painter who finished has achieved the value, so the state can proceed from that achievement. Announcing a project is not achieving it. Stopping in the name of a higher renunciation gives up the value rather than realizing it. A rule unrelated to the work cannot award the state to either of them, because the state is not a prize detached from what was done.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that names the source of happiness.

feedback.note: Happiness proceeds from the achievement of one's values. The renunciation of those values does not produce the state, and a mere wish is not an achievement, because nothing has yet been gained or kept. The order is achievement first and the state as what follows. Reversing it asks for an effect while removing the cause.

exercises.prompt: Which order is the cause, and which is the effect?

choices.text: Happiness is the cause, and one's life is rearranged to fit the feeling
The two may be swapped, because a feeling can define the life
One's life, and the rational values it requires, are the cause. Happiness is the effect
Neither comes first, because happiness is an undefined primary

feedback.note: Life is the cause and happiness is the concomitant, because one achieves happiness by accepting man's life as primary and pursuing the values it requires. Taking the feeling as an undefined primary reverses the order. The two may not be swapped. A feeling does not tell one what the life requires. It registers the success or failure of the values one has or has not achieved.

exercises.prompt: A woman chases a pleasant mood first and says her life will be whatever the mood demands. What has she reversed?

choices.text: Cause and effect. She took happiness as a primary and tried to live by its guidance
Nothing, because a mood is man's life
Only her schedule, which has no moral meaning
The renunciation of her values, which is the proper cause

feedback.note: She reversed cause and effect, because the mood is an effect of achieved values and cannot be the guide that selects them. Man's life is the primary, not the feeling. The chase is not a neutral schedule. It is an attempt to live by an undefined happiness. Renouncing her values would not repair the reversal. It would remove the cause the effect depends on.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its place in the order.

pairs.left: Man's life, accepted as primary
The rational values that life requires
pairs.right: What one pursues in order to live

pairs.left: Happiness
pairs.right: The state that follows, not the guide

feedback.note: One accepts man's life as primary, pursues the rational values it requires, and experiences happiness as the effect, because the relationship of cause to effect cannot be reversed. Happiness is the concomitant of that pursuit, not the standard that directs it. Starting from an undefined feeling leaves the pursuit with no cause.

exercises.prompt: Complete the thing one must accept as primary.

feedback.note: Man's life is the primary, because happiness is achieved by pursuing the rational values that life requires, not by consulting an undefined feeling. A whim, the feeling, and renunciation are attempts to start from the effect or from its destruction. They do not identify what one must accept first.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about trying to live by happiness as a primary?

exercises.prompt: A hedonist says, "I do not need to know what my life requires. I will know the good by whether it feels like happiness." Why is that empty?

choices.text: It is not empty, because a feeling is a complete guide
The feeling is the effect. Used as a guide before any value is judged, it has no content
It is empty only because happiness is a possession, not a state
It is the same claim as accepting man's life as primary

feedback.note: The feeling cannot guide the choice that is supposed to produce it, because until one knows what one's life requires there is no value whose achievement the feeling could register. Hedonism treats an undefined happiness as a primary. That is not the same claim as holding man's life as the cause. The state remains a state. The error is using it as the standard.

exercises.prompt: Which practice respects the order of cause and effect?

choices.text: Choose the values man's life requires, achieve them, and take the resulting state as the reward
Choose whichever glow is strongest, then invent values that match it
Renounce one's values so the glow will have nothing to contradict
Treat the glow as the standard and one's life as optional

feedback.note: The respectful practice starts from man's life, achieves the values it requires, and receives happiness as the effect, because that is the order that cannot be reversed. Inventing values to match a glow, renouncing values, and treating life as optional all take the feeling as primary. They ask the effect to do the work of the cause.

exercises.prompt: Build the order that keeps the cause in front of the effect.

feedback.note: Hold man's life as primary, pursue the values it requires, and happiness follows. Taking happiness as primary reverses the cause, and renouncing one's values removes the pursuit, because the state is a concomitant of achieving rational values rather than a substitute for them. Life remains the cause.

exercises.prompt: Why is happiness not a whim or an undefined urge?

choices.text: A whim has no tie to an achieved value. Happiness proceeds from values one has achieved
A whim is the standard of value, and happiness is the same standard
Happiness is any pleasant sensation, including one that destroys one's life
Happiness requires a clash with one's values, and a whim supplies the clash

feedback.note: Happiness is not a whim, because a whim is a desire with no tie to a value one's life requires, while the state proceeds from values actually achieved. It is not the standard of value. Man's life is. A destructive pleasant sensation and a clash with one's values are the kinds of feeling the state is not. They do not become happiness by being wanted.

exercises.prompt: A man calls a passing urge his happiness and says the urge, not his life, is what makes an action good. Which two errors is he making?

choices.text: None. An urge is both the state and the standard
He confuses a whim with a possession, and nothing further
He treats a whim as happiness, and he treats happiness as the standard of value
He accepts man's life as primary and only misnames the reward

feedback.note: He makes both errors, because a passing urge is not the state that proceeds from achieved values, and neither the urge nor that state is the standard. The standard remains man's life. He has not merely mislabeled a reward while keeping the cause straight. He has put a whim in the place of the cause. A possession is a different confusion, and it is not the one he stated.

exercises.prompt: Match each feeling to the name it does or does not deserve.

pairs.left: Joy that comes from achieving a real value, with no betrayal of one's other values
A desire with no tie to any value one's life requires
Pleasure taken in faking reality

feedback.note: Happiness is the joy of achieving real values, and it does not clash with the rest of what one holds, because the state proceeds from those values rather than from their betrayal. A whim lacks the tie to a value. Pleasure in a fake is the joy of escaping reality, not of achieving it. Wanting the pleasure does not rename it.

State, reward, and effect are names for what happiness is, under man's life as the cause. Putting them in the blank would deny the principle rather than state it.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the joy that counts as happiness?
exercises.quote: Happiness is a state of non-contradictory joy—a joy without penalty or guilt, a joy that does not clash with any of your values and does not work for your own destruction, not the joy of escaping from your mind, but of using your mind's fullest power, not the joy of faking reality, but of achieving values that are real, not the joy of a drunkard, but of a producer.

Happiness is non-contradictory joy from achieving real values by using one's mind

Happiness is the joy of escaping one's mind

feedback.quote: Happiness is a state of non-contradictory joy—a joy without penalty or guilt, a joy that does not clash with any of your values and does not work for your own destruction, not the joy of escaping from your mind, but of using your mind's fullest power, not the joy of faking reality, but of achieving values that are real, not the joy of a drunkard, but of a producer.

feedback.note: The passage describes non-contradictory joy: no penalty, no guilt, no clash with one's values, the joy of using one's mind and of achieving values that are real, not the joy of a drunkard or of faking reality. Escaping one's mind is the opposite of that description. A clash with one's values is what the passage rules out, because the joy would then work for one's own destruction.

exercises.prompt: Why can happiness not be the standard of value, even though it is the emotional reward of living well?

choices.text: Because a reward is always the measure of what one should choose
Because man's life is an effect, and the feeling is the cause
Because only a whim is allowed to judge an action
Because the standard is what man's survival as a rational being requires, and the state is a result

feedback.note: The standard is man's life, what survival as a rational being requires, and happiness is the state that results from achieving the values that life requires. A result cannot be the measure that selects the values, because the measure has to be known before the result exists. Treating the reward as the standard is the reversal already rejected. A whim is not a permitted substitute for the standard.

exercises.prompt: A policy says, "Betray the work you value whenever a pleasant impulse appears, and call the impulse happiness." What two claims does it confuse?

choices.text: A whim with happiness, and a betrayal with the achievement of a value
Man's life with the standard, which is the confusion
A real achievement with joy, which is the confusion
Pride with productiveness, and nothing about happiness

feedback.note: The impulse is a whim, not happiness, and the betrayal is not an achievement, because happiness proceeds from values one keeps rather than from values one sells for a feeling. Holding man's life as the standard is not the confusion. It is the correction. Joy at a real achievement is the state, not the error. The policy never reaches the virtues. It fails earlier, at the cause of the state.

exercises.prompt: Build the double rejection of whim and of a false standard.

feedback.note: Happiness is not a whim, and it is not the standard of value. A destructive glow and a clash with one's values are further things the state is not, because the joy at issue comes from achieving real values and does not work for one's destruction. The standard remains man's life. The state remains the effect of living by the values that standard requires.

exercises.prompt: Which statement holds the whole account of happiness?

choices.text: Happiness is a whim, the standard of value, and the reward for renouncing one's values
It is the state of consciousness that proceeds from achieved values, with life as the cause
It is a possession one earns by betraying the work one's life requires
It is a rule one obeys by taking an undefined feeling as primary

feedback.note: The whole account is a state of consciousness proceeding from achieved values, because one holds man's life as primary and pursues the values it requires. A whim, a betrayal, and an undefined feeling each drop a part of that account. Happiness is the reward of the achievement, not the standard that selects it, and renunciation does not produce it.

exercises.prompt: An artist gives up the work she values most in order to chase a pleasant mood, and she calls the chase her moral purpose. What has she lost?

choices.text: The cause. The mood is not achieved by renouncing the value, and it is not the standard
Nothing, if the mood is pleasant
Only a possession, which the mood replaces at equal worth
The duty to take happiness as an undefined primary

feedback.note: She has dropped the cause, because happiness proceeds from achieving her values, and she is renouncing the central one in order to chase a feeling. The feeling is not the standard. Man's life is, and the work was a value that life required. A pleasant mood does not replace the work at equal worth. The undefined primary is the error, not a duty she failed.

Achieved values

Happiness is the resulting state, which is also the emotional form of one's moral purpose, not a second standard. A whim and a renunciation produce neither the cause nor the state, because one is empty and the other gives the values up.

exercises.prompt: A critic says, "If happiness is the moral purpose, then any whim that feels happy is the good." What did he collapse?

Holding life as the cause is the correction, not the error. The virtues are not what he confused. He treated an effect as if it could be any feeling and could judge the action that is supposed to produce it.

exercises.prompt: Which life is aimed at happiness in the sense the account allows?

choices.text: She picks a destructive pleasure, calls it the standard, and renounces her work

Destructive pleasure, a collection of compliments, and commanded joy during a betrayal each skip the achievement. They want the reward of a life they are not living.

feedback.note: Life is the cause, achieved values are what one pursues, and happiness is the state that follows. A whim is not the standard, and renunciation is not the method, because the state proceeds from values one achieves under man's life as primary. The moral purpose is the achievement of one's own happiness, understood in that order and not as a license to start from a feeling.

exercises.prompt: What does the idea of value presuppose, before any particular good is named?

choices.text: An entity that faces an alternative, so something can be gained or lost
