feedback.note: Value presupposes an entity facing an alternative, because only then is there something it can act to gain or keep. Where nothing can be lost, nothing is a value. A feeling or a command, offered with no such entity, skips the condition that makes the concept possible.

exercises.prompt: A rock rests in a quarry. Does the rock have values of its own?

Yes, if observers agree to treat the rock as a chooser
No. It faces no alternative of life or nonexistence, so nothing is a value to it

feedback.note: The rock has no values of its own because it faces no alternative: it does not stand to go out of existence as a living thing does. Existence alone is not a value. Observers cannot vote a valuer into a stone. A person may value the stone as a resource, but that value belongs to the living valuers, not to the rock.

Where there is no alternative, there are no values. Treating a stone as a valuer confuses existence with a stake, because a stone does not face life or death.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says, "Whatever exists is a value to itself, so a stone values being a stone." What is the error?

feedback.note: Existence is not the same fact as value, because value starts only where an entity faces an alternative. The stone does not face life or death, so it does not value being a stone. A living person can still value the stone as a means to his life. Denying that would confuse the stone's lack of values with a ban on using stones.

exercises.prompt: Someone says a thing is good only because he feels like it, with no life at stake. What has he dropped?

choices.text: The alternative that makes value possible, and put a feeling in its place
Nothing, because a feeling is the fundamental alternative
The duty to ignore whatever his life requires
The claim that inanimate matter faces death

feedback.note: A feeling is not the root of value, because value presupposes an entity facing an alternative, and for a living organism that alternative is life or death. Subjectivism puts a feeling in place of that stake. The error does not consist in refusing to call rocks mortal, and it does not make ignoring one's life a duty.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that ties value to life.

feedback.note: Value presupposes an alternative, and for a living organism that alternative is life or death. A mere feeling does not create the stake, because a feeling is not the alternative of existing or ceasing. Denying the alternative removes values rather than explaining them. Where nothing can be gained or lost, the concept does not arise.

exercises.prompt: Where do the concepts of good and evil come from?

choices.text: From objects that are good or evil with no living being involved
From the alternative of life or death, which only a living organism faces
From a feeling that does not refer to any life
From a command that forbids asking what sustains a life

feedback.note: Good and evil arise only where the alternative is life or death, because only then does an organism have something to gain or lose. What sustains its life is the good, and what threatens that life is the evil. A feeling, a baseless command, or a good supposedly sitting in an object with no valuer all skip that alternative.

exercises.prompt: A storm destroys a crop. In what sense, if any, is the storm evil?

choices.text: It is disastrous for the living, but it is not a moral agent choosing against a life
It is morally wicked because nature owes farmers an easy season
It is morally good because destruction is a value
It is neither good nor bad for anyone, because crops are not alive

feedback.note: The storm can be bad for living beings whose lives depend on the crop, because their alternative is life or death. The storm itself does not choose, so it is not a moral agent to praise or blame. Calling nature wicked treats a metaphysically given fact as a vice. Calling the crop unrelated to life ignores the organism the crop was for.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the evaluation that fits it.

pairs.left: Food that keeps an organism alive
A poison that ends that life
A rock, considered as a moral agent
pairs.right: Neither morally good nor morally evil

feedback.note: Good and evil are measured by life or death. What keeps the organism alive is good for it, and what ends that life is evil for it. A rock is neither, because it does not face the alternative and does not choose. The words do not float free of a living being.

exercises.prompt: Complete the alternative that makes good and evil possible.

feedback.note: Death completes the alternative, because life is a process that can fail, and that stake is what makes good and evil possible. Fashion, applause, and custom are social substitutes. They do not give an organism something it must gain or lose in order to go on existing.

exercises.prompt: A physician offers a bitter medicine that will save a patient's life. By the alternative of life or death, what is the medicine?

choices.text: Evil, because it is unpleasant
Neither, because only pleasant things can be good

feedback.note: The medicine is good for the patient's life because it supports the life rather than destroying it. Unpleasantness is not the alternative that defines evil. A crowd's taste is a further substitute, and it does not change what the organism needs in order to keep existing.

exercises.prompt: An intrinsicist says a gem is good in itself, with no reference to any organism's life. What is missing?

choices.text: Nothing, because good is a feature sealed inside objects

A command that the gem be praised whether or not it serves a life
A living being for whom the gem could be a gain or a loss

feedback.note: Nothing is good in itself apart from a life it can serve, because good and evil arise only from the alternative a living organism faces. Intrinsicism drops that valuer and treats value as a revelation in the object, with no method and no stake. A feeling or a command would not put the missing life back into the theory.

exercises.prompt: A man calls gravity evil because he wanted to fly by wishing. Which distinction does he miss?

Gravity is good because limits are always virtues

feedback.note: Gravity is a fact of identity, not a moral agent, so disliking it does not make it evil. Moral good and evil apply where a choosing being faces life or death and acts for or against that life. Calling every unwanted fact a vice erases that distinction. A wish does not rewrite the fact, and it does not turn the fact into a moral choice.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim about where good and evil arise.

feedback.note: Good and evil arise only where the alternative is life or death. A private feeling does not create that alternative, and an intrinsic glow treats value as sealed in an object with no organism at stake. Both substitutes fail because they do not say what the living being stands to gain or lose.

exercises.prompt: What is the root of value, as against a whim, a vote, or a supernatural order?

A whim is subjectivism, a vote is a social substitute for that root, and a revealed command is mysticism. None of them is the alternative of life or death, so none of them can ground good and evil.

exercises.prompt: A buyer says a fraud is good because he feels clever, and he offers no other ground. Which view is this?

The view that good and evil come from life or death

The life-or-death alternative is what he dropped. The stone example is a different error, about inanimate matter, and it is not the claim he made.

exercises.prompt: Match each rival to the root of value it puts in place of life.

Mysticism offers a command with no tie to what a life requires. Intrinsicism treats the good as revealed in the object, so no method and no organism are needed. Life is the root they all drop.

feedback.note: Life is the root, because only a living organism faces the alternative that makes value possible. Feeling, fashion, and revelation are the substitutes: a whim, a crowd, and a mystical command. Putting any of them in the blank states the error rather than the principle.

exercises.prompt: A committee declares a project good because the majority wants it, and it refuses to ask what anyone's life requires. What is the error?

exercises.prompt: A preacher says a deed is good because a vision ordered it, and you must not ask whether it sustains anyone's life. What is he offering?

exercises.prompt: Kantian wording: duty binds even when it destroys the agent's life, and life is irrelevant to the moral test. Why does that fail as a root of value?

It is not saved by calling the destruction noble, and it is not the same error as a whim, though both abandon life as the standard's basis.

"Whatever feels intense" is the whim again. All of them fail because they do not rest on the alternative of life or death.

exercises.prompt: Which formulation keeps the standard of value distinct from the ethical purpose?

exercises.prompt: A man says his standard is whatever he feels like calling "my life" today. What has he collapsed?

The purpose remains his own life, but a purpose does not license him to treat a mood as the measure of good and evil. Other people's lives are not the standard he was asked to use.

exercises.prompt: Match each role to the claim that belongs to it.

Neither substitute is the same claim as the standard or the purpose, because each changes what is being measured or for whom.

He turned the standard into a collective and replaced one's own life as the purpose
He reduced the standard to a whim, which is what the state forbids

feedback.note: Man's life, as the standard, means what a human being needs in order to survive as a rational being, not the life of a state. The purpose is each person's own life. The speaker replaced both, because a collective is not the standard and service to it is not the purpose. That is a social substitute, not a restatement.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the standard of value and the ethical purpose?
exercises.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds man's life as the standard of value—and his own life as the ethical purpose of every individual man.

choices.text: One's own whim is the standard, and mankind is the purpose
The standard and the purpose are both the collective life of society
There is a purpose and no standard, because good and evil are feelings
Man's life is the standard of value, and one's own life is the ethical purpose

feedback.quote: The Objectivist ethics holds man's life as the standard of value—and his own life as the ethical purpose of every individual man.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 23
feedback.note: The passage holds the two claims apart, because man's life is the standard of value and one's own life is the ethical purpose of each person. A whim is not the standard, and society is not the purpose. Dropping the standard and keeping a feeling would erase the measure by which a person judges what his own life requires.

exercises.prompt: Someone says survival at any price, including a life that refuses to think, meets the standard. What does "as a rational being" rule out?

choices.text: Any concern with remaining alive
Bare physical persistence by means that abandon reason
The purpose of one's own life, which must be replaced by a crowd
Judging an action by what a human life requires

feedback.note: The standard is man's survival as a rational being, not mere duration, because means that abandon reason fail it even if the heart keeps beating. One's own life remains the purpose. The error does not ban wanting to live, and it does not make a person the servant of a crowd.

exercises.prompt: Build the two-part principle in the order that keeps the halves distinct.

feedback.note: Man's life is the standard, and one's own life is the purpose. A whim cannot fill the standard's place, because the standard is what survival as a rational being requires. The collective cannot fill the purpose's place, because the purpose is the individual's own life. Putting either substitute in collapses a half of the principle.

exercises.prompt: When is an action morally good, and when is it morally evil?

choices.text: Good when it sustains one's own life as a rational being, evil when it works against that life
Good when it is pleasant, evil when it is difficult
Good when a crowd approves, evil when the agent benefits
Good when it sacrifices one's life, evil when it keeps that life

feedback.note: An action is good when it sustains one's own life by the standard of what a rational being's survival requires, and evil when it works against that life. Pleasure, difficulty, and a crowd's vote are not that standard. Praising the destruction of one's life inverts good and evil, because it treats the purpose as something to be surrendered.

exercises.prompt: A fraud keeps a man fed for a month and destroys his honesty and his victims' work. How does the standard judge it?

choices.text: Good, because his body was fed
Neither, because money is outside moral judgment
Evil, because it works against life as a rational being, his and theirs
Good, because a feeling of cleverness is the standard

feedback.note: Feeding the body by faking reality does not meet the standard, because man's life means survival as a rational being, not a month of loot. The fraud works against the agent's own life as that kind of being and against the victims. A clever feeling is a whim, not the measure. Money is not outside judgment. The means are exactly what the standard judges.

exercises.prompt: Match each action to the judgment the standard supports.

pairs.left: Productive work one chose because it sustains one's life
A fraud that buys comfort by faking reality
A painful treatment that preserves the life one values
pairs.right: For one's life, despite the pain

feedback.note: The standard asks whether the action sustains one's own life as a rational being, not whether it is pleasant. Chosen productive work does. A fraud works against that life even if it buys comfort. Painful treatment can be for one's life when it preserves the life one values, because the pain is a cost and the life is the stake.

exercises.prompt: Complete the measure used to judge an action.

parts.text: Judge an action by whether it sustains or works against one's own life as a

feedback.note: A rational being names the standard, because the life at stake is man's survival as the kind of being who lives by reason. A passing mood, a public vote, and a revealed order are the substitutes already rejected as roots of value. They do not tell you whether the action serves your life or works against it.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the standard by which one judges good and evil?
exercises.quote: The standard of value of the Objectivist ethics—the standard by which one judges what is good or evil—is man's life, or: that which is required for man's survival qua man.

choices.text: The standard is whatever keeps the body going, by any means
The standard is man's life: what man's survival as a rational being requires
The standard is a whim, and survival is irrelevant
The standard is the collective, and one's own life is an obstacle

feedback.quote: The standard of value of the Objectivist ethics—the standard by which one judges what is good or evil—is man's life, or: that which is required for man's survival qua man.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 23
feedback.note: The passage says the standard by which one judges good or evil is man's life, because that means what man's survival as a rational being requires. Bare persistence by any means drops the kind of survival at stake. A whim and a collective are not the standard the passage names. One's own life is the purpose, not a replacement for the standard.

exercises.prompt: A dependent refuses to think and lives by seizing other people's work, yet he is still breathing. Does he meet the standard?

choices.text: Yes, because breathing is the whole of man's life
Yes, because the victims' loss is outside the standard
Yes, if he feels safe
No. Survival as a rational being is not mindless persistence by robbery

feedback.note: Breathing by refusing to think and by robbery fails the standard, because the standard is survival as a rational being, not duration at any price. The action works against his own life in that sense and against the lives of the people he seizes from. A feeling of safety does not rewrite the measure. The purpose is his own life, and these means do not sustain it as a human life.

exercises.prompt: An engineer tells an inconvenient truth because faking the report would corrupt the judgment his work requires. The truth costs him a contract. Which way does the action point?

choices.text: Toward his life, because the cost buys nothing that outranks the mind he lives by
Against his life, because any loss is evil
Against his life, because a contract is the standard of value
Neither way, because truth is a social ornament

feedback.note: The action sustains his life as a rational being, because his judgment is what that life depends on, and the lost contract does not outrank it. Calling every loss evil confuses a cost with a betrayal of one's life. A contract is not the standard. Truth is not an ornament added after the work. The work itself required the judgment he refused to fake.

exercises.prompt: A woman gives up her own life's central work to serve a stranger's project, solely because she is told that her life is not a purpose. How should that be judged?

choices.text: Good, because one's own life must not be the purpose
Good, because the standard is the collective and never the requirements of a rational life
Evil, because it works against her life and replaces her purpose with a command
Neither, because purpose and standard are whims

feedback.note: The purpose is her own life, and the standard is what a rational being's survival requires. Dropping the work her life depends on, for a stranger taken as a duty, works against that life, because the command denies that her life is a purpose. Calling the collective the measure does not repair it, and a whim does not do the judging.

exercises.prompt: Which list is the code of virtues, in the order that keeps rationality first?

choices.text: Faith, hope, charity, mercy, obedience, humility, and sacrifice
Rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride
Reason, purpose, and self-esteem, offered as the whole code of virtues
Rationality, productiveness, and pride, with the other four dropped as optional

feedback.note: The seven are rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride, because they are one code and rationality is the primary virtue. The theological list is a different morality. Reason, purpose, and self-esteem are the cardinal values, not the virtues. The three corresponding virtues do not license dropping the other four.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean that rationality is primary?

choices.text: The other virtues are rationality applied to particular choices, not rivals of it
Rationality is the first word on a list and may be skipped in action
Rationality replaces the need for honesty, justice, and the rest
Primary means whatever a crowd puts at the top of its own list

feedback.note: Rationality is primary because the other virtues are applications of reason to particular choices: to other people's judgment, to one's own action, to facts, to desert, to work, and to one's character. Skipping it in action drops the source. It does not make the other six unnecessary, and a crowd does not get to rename the primary.

exercises.prompt: Match each virtue to the choice it governs.

pairs.left: Independence
pairs.right: Forming one's own judgment, with reality as the orientation

pairs.left: Integrity
pairs.right: Acting on the rational judgment one has reached

pairs.left: Honesty
Justice
pairs.right: Judging people by the facts and treating them as they deserve

feedback.note: These four are distinct applications of rationality, because whose judgment, whether one acts on it, whether one fakes facts, and how one treats people are different choices. None of them is an eighth virtue added from outside the code. None of them replaces rationality, since each is reason used on a particular question.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of the virtue the others depend on.

parts.text: The primary virtue is

feedback.note: Rationality is primary, because the other virtues are reason applied to particular choices, and without it they have no source. Mercy, faith, and sacrifice are not names for that source. Treating any of them as primary would replace the code with a different morality, one that does not take reason as the judge of action.

exercises.prompt: A teacher adds "unearned mercy for everyone" as an eighth virtue. What is wrong with the addition?

choices.text: Nothing, because a code may grow any virtue a feeling recommends
The error is including justice, which already demands equal outcomes
The error is keeping rationality, which forbids judging people
The code has seven virtues, and unearned mercy is not one of them

feedback.note: There is no eighth virtue, because the code is the seven, and justice is judging people by the facts rather than granting the unearned. Unearned mercy as a duty contradicts justice. It does not follow from rationality. A feeling does not get to appoint a new virtue, and justice does not demand equal outcomes.

exercises.prompt: Someone keeps only rationality, productiveness, and pride, and calls independence, integrity, honesty, and justice optional manners. What has he done?

choices.text: He has stated the full code, because only three virtues exist
He has confused virtues with the cardinal values, but the remaining four are still in his code
He has shrunk the code to the three corresponding virtues and dropped four applications of rationality
He has added an eighth virtue by shortening the list

feedback.note: The three corresponding virtues are part of the seven, not a shorter code, because independence, integrity, honesty, and justice are rationality applied to further choices. Dropping them as manners removes virtues, it does not add an eighth. They are not the cardinal values under new names. The full code is still the seven.

exercises.prompt: A list begins with obedience and never mentions rationality. Can it be this code under a new opening word?

choices.text: Yes, because the primary virtue is whichever word comes first
No. A code that does not take reason as primary is not this code
Yes, if obedience is renamed rationality after the list is memorized
No, only because the list has fewer than seven words, whatever the words are

feedback.note: Obedience is not rationality, and a list that starts by setting reason aside is a different morality, because this code takes reason as one's only guide to action. Renaming obedience later does not insert the virtue. The count of words is not the objection. The objection is the missing primary, without which the other virtues have nothing to apply.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim that the virtues are one code.

feedback.note: The seven virtues are one code, and rationality is primary. An eighth virtue is an invention, and a license to drop four treats the corresponding virtues of the cardinal values as if they were the whole code. Both fail because the code is exactly these seven, with the others as applications of rationality rather than optional manners.

exercises.prompt: What is the virtue of rationality, stated as a policy?

choices.text: Accepting reason as one's only source of knowledge, judge of values, and guide to action
Using one's mind to make a wish look like a fact
Repeating a group's conclusion because the group is confident
Feeling strongly, and treating the feeling as the judge of value

feedback.note: Rationality accepts reason as one's only source of knowledge, only judge of values, and only guide to action, because that is what it means to practice the primary virtue. Rationalizing fakes a fact in reason's name. A borrowed conclusion skips the knowing. A feeling is not a judge of values. All three refuse the virtue they may claim to honor.

exercises.prompt: Before acting, a builder checks his plan against the measurements and changes the plan. Which virtue is he practicing first?

choices.text: A refusal of reason, because he did not trust his first wish
Rationalizing, because he used his mind on a practical question
Rationality, because the facts are his guide and his values are judged by them
Obedience, because a measurement is a command from the materials

feedback.note: He is practicing rationality, because he lets reason judge the plan and guide the action. Changing a wish when the facts require it is the virtue, not a refusal of it. Using one's mind on a practical question is not rationalizing. Rationalizing would be arranging words to protect the original wish. A measurement is evidence, not a mystical command.

exercises.prompt: Match each policy to the name that fits it.

pairs.left: Face the facts and let them guide the choice
Blank out a fact one does not want to see
Invent a story so a wish will look proven

feedback.note: Rationality is the policy of facing the facts and being guided by them. Evasion blanks a fact out, so reason is not used at all. Rationalizing uses the mind to fake support for a wish, which is a counterfeit of the virtue, because the conclusion was protected from the evidence rather than drawn from it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the office rationality gives to reason.

parts.text: Rationality takes reason as one's only guide to

feedback.note: Action is what reason has to guide, because rationality is not a spectator's compliment to the faculty. It is the policy of choosing by what one knows. Evasion, fashion, and revelation are substitutes that do not guide action by identification of the facts. They are ways of refusing the primary virtue.

exercises.prompt: A team repeats a conclusion none of them can explain, because the senior person is sure. Which virtue fails first?

choices.text: None, because confidence in a group is a form of reason
Productiveness only, because no material was moved
Pride only, because the conclusion may still be true
Rationality, because reason is not being used as the means of knowledge

feedback.note: Rationality fails first, because one's only source of knowledge is reason, and repeating an unexplained conclusion is not knowing it. The conclusion might happen to be true, and that still does not make the repetition rational. Confidence is not evidence. Other virtues may fail as well, but the primary breach is the refusal to use one's own mind on the facts.

exercises.prompt: New evidence refutes a conclusion one liked. Refusing to revise is defended as "being rational enough already." What is the defense?

choices.text: A real practice of rationality, because the first conclusion must be loyal
A breach of rationality, because reason requires one to follow the new evidence
Integrity, which consists in never changing a judgment
Independence, which consists in ignoring facts other people noticed

feedback.note: Rationality requires revising a refuted conclusion, because reason is one's only means of knowledge and the new evidence is knowledge one must integrate. Loyalty to the first conclusion, against the facts, is evasion or rationalizing. Integrity does not mean never changing one's mind. Independence does not mean ignoring facts, whoever noticed them.

exercises.prompt: An investor calls a strong hunch his judge of value and says the figures are optional. Which clause of rationality has he dropped?

choices.text: Reason as his only judge of values, replaced by a feeling
Nothing, if the hunch is intense
Only productiveness, which is the same virtue as a hunch
The right to act, which rationality forbids

feedback.note: He has dropped reason as his only judge of values, because a hunch is a feeling and the figures are the facts the judgment has to integrate. Intensity does not promote the feeling into a standard. Productiveness is a different virtue, and it depends on rationality rather than replacing it. Rationality exists to guide action, not to forbid it.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement of the primary virtue.

feedback.note: Rationality accepts reason as one's only guide to knowledge, value, and action. Using it as a tool for faking is rationalizing, and treating it as optional when inconvenient is evasion. Both fail because the virtue is unconditional within its office: reason remains the only source, the only judge, and the only guide.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between independence and integrity?

choices.text: There is none. Both mean never listening to another person
Independence means acting, and integrity means letting others form one's conclusions
Independence forms one's own judgment. Integrity acts on the rational judgment formed
Integrity means never revising a view, and independence means ignoring facts

feedback.note: Independence is the virtue of forming one's own judgments, with reality rather than other people as one's orientation. Integrity is the virtue of acting on the rational judgment one has reached. They are not the same choice, because one can think for oneself and then fail to act, or act firmly on a conclusion one never judged. Never listening, and never revising, are caricatures of both.

exercises.prompt: A student grasps the evidence and then accepts a scientist's result. Has independence failed?

choices.text: No. Independence orients one to reality, and understanding the evidence is that orientation
Yes, because any agreement with another person is dependence
Yes, because independence requires one to reject true conclusions
No, only because the scientist's prestige was the student's reason

feedback.note: Independence does not forbid learning, because the orientation is to reality, and evidence is reality's claim. Accepting a result one understands is using one's own mind. Automatic rejection would be a pose, not the virtue. Prestige as the reason would fail independence, but that is not the case described. The student judged the evidence.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the virtue it keeps or drops.

pairs.left: Judges by the evidence, then does what that judgment requires
Knows the right action and does the opposite to please a client
Acts with great firmness on a slogan he never understood

feedback.note: Thinking for oneself and acting on that thought are different virtues, and both are required. Pleasing a client against one's judgment drops integrity, because one is sacrificing a conviction to another person's wish. Firmness on an ununderstood slogan drops independence, because the action has no judgment of one's own behind it. Firmness does not substitute for either virtue.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two questions these virtues answer.

parts.text: Independence asks whose
forms the judgment, and integrity asks whether one
on it.

feedback.note: Mind names the question independence answers, and acts names the question integrity answers, because one virtue forms the judgment and the other lives by it. An audience and an impulse do not fill either job. One can judge by one's own mind and still fail to act, which drops integrity without erasing the independence of the thinking.

exercises.prompt: A designer knows a structure is unsafe and signs the plan anyway, to keep a contract. Which virtue fails, even if the thinking was his own?

choices.text: Independence only, because signing is a way of forming a judgment
Neither, if the contract is large
Rationality only, and integrity has nothing to say about action
Integrity, because he acts against the rational judgment he reached

feedback.note: Integrity fails, because he had reached a judgment and then sacrificed it to a contract. Independence may already have done its work in the thinking. The size of the contract does not change the betrayal. Rationality was needed to reach the judgment, but the distinctive breach in the signing is the refusal to act on what he knows. That is what integrity names.

exercises.prompt: After his view is refuted, a man keeps it so he will look consistent. He calls the stubbornness integrity. What is it?

choices.text: Integrity, because consistency against the facts is the virtue
A breach of rationality posing as integrity. Integrity follows a rational judgment, including a revised one
Independence, because ignoring a refutation orients one to reality
Pride, which consists in never admitting an error

feedback.note: Integrity is loyalty to one's rational convictions, not loyalty to a refuted sentence, because a conviction that contradicts the facts is no longer rational. Keeping it to look consistent betrays rationality and then calls the betrayal integrity. Independence does not mean ignoring refutations. Pride does not mean refusing to admit an error. It means earning the right to a judgment one can still defend.

exercises.prompt: A rebel rejects every conclusion other people hold, including those he can see are true, and calls that independence. What has he substituted?

choices.text: Other people, as a negative guide, in place of reality
Nothing, because independence is the refusal of true conclusions
Integrity, which requires him to act against his own eyes
Rationality, practiced by systematic disagreement

feedback.note: Independence takes reality as one's primary orientation, not other people, either as authorities or as targets. Systematic disagreement is still other-directed, because the rebel's guide is "not what they think" rather than "what the facts are." It is not integrity, and it is not rationality. Both of those require one to follow the evidence one actually has.

exercises.prompt: Which person has kept both independence and integrity?

choices.text: She copies a famous verdict she cannot explain, then follows it at great cost
He judges the evidence correctly and then acts against it to be liked
She judges by the facts, including facts others found, and she acts on that judgment
He never revises, and he never asks what the facts are

feedback.note: Both virtues are present only when the judgment is one's own, formed by reference to reality, and the action follows it. Copying an unexplained verdict fails independence even if the later action is costly. Acting against a true judgment fails integrity. Refusing to look fails rationality and both of these virtues with it, because there is no rational conviction to form or to practice.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between honesty and justice?

choices.text: Honesty judges people, and justice is a duty to announce every thought
Honesty refuses to fake reality. Justice judges people by the facts and treats them as they deserve
They are the same virtue, and both demand equal outcomes
Justice is unearned mercy as a duty, and honesty is whatever keeps the peace

feedback.note: Honesty is the refusal to fake reality, to oneself or to others, because the unreal is unreal and cannot be made a value by pretending. Justice is about people: judge them by the facts and treat them as they deserve. Equal outcomes ignore those facts. Unearned mercy as a duty grants what has not been earned. Announcing every thought is not what honesty demands.

exercises.prompt: A woman keeps a private plan to herself and does not pretend the plan is something else. Has she broken honesty?

choices.text: No. Honesty forbids faking, not privacy. She has not pretended the false is true
Yes, because honesty is the duty to announce every thought
Yes, if someone else would have preferred to hear the plan
No, only because privacy is a form of lying that justice requires

feedback.note: Honesty is the refusal to fake reality, not a duty to disclose every thought, because silence is not the same act as pretending. She has not claimed the plan is other than it is. Another person's curiosity does not create that duty. Calling privacy a required lie would invert the virtue. Justice, likewise, does not demand that every mental content be published.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to the virtue it breaches or keeps.

pairs.left: Publishing figures one knows are false
Keeping a private conclusion and not asserting its opposite
Rewarding a default and an achievement with the same pay
Admiring a producer for work he actually did

feedback.note: Honesty is about whether reality is faked, so a false report breaches it and a private unspoken conclusion does not. Justice is about whether people are judged and treated by the facts. Equal pay for unequal achievement ignores desert, and admiration for real work grants what was earned. The two virtues are not interchangeable, because one polices pretense and the other polices desert.

exercises.prompt: Complete the statements of honesty and of justice.

parts.text: Honesty refuses to fake
, and justice treats people as they

feedback.note: Reality is what honesty refuses to fake, and deserve is the measure justice uses, because one virtue concerns facts and the other concerns how people are treated in light of the facts. Applause and equally do not complete either clause. Equal treatment without regard to the facts is the error justice rejects, not the virtue itself.

exercises.prompt: A manager pays every employee the same, including those who produced and those who did not, and calls the sameness justice. What is it?

choices.text: Justice, because equal outcomes are what desert means
Honesty, because a payroll is a way of announcing every thought
Justice, if the manager feels merciful
A breach of justice, because people are not being treated as their actions deserve

feedback.note: Justice judges people by the facts and treats them as they deserve, so identical pay for production and for default ignores the facts. Equal outcomes are not desert. A merciful feeling does not rewrite what was earned. Honesty is not the virtue at issue. The payroll is not a confession of thoughts. It is a distribution, and the distribution is unjust.

exercises.prompt: A judge is told that mercy, as a duty, requires him to clear a person the evidence shows is guilty. What would compliance be?

choices.text: Justice, because mercy for the guilty is the same thing as desert
Honesty, because clearing the guilty refuses to fake reality
A breach of justice. Unearned mercy is not a duty, and the facts are the measure
Independence, because a duty from outside replaces his judgment properly

feedback.note: Compliance would breach justice, because the person would be treated better than the facts deserve, and unearned mercy is not a moral debt. It would also pressure honesty if the clearing required him to pretend the evidence says something else. Independence does not consist in handing one's judgment to a duty. The facts remain the measure of what the person deserves.

exercises.prompt: A salesman knows the product fails and describes it as sound in order to be paid. Which virtues fail, and why is honesty not optional politeness?

choices.text: Only justice toward himself, because the customer's knowledge is not a fact
Honesty, because he fakes reality, and the pay is not a value he can count on as real
Neither, if the customer feels pleased for an hour
Pride only, which consists in successful pretense

feedback.note: Honesty fails because he pretends the false is true, and a value obtained that way is not a value his life can rely on. The unreal does not become real when the customer is briefly pleased. Justice is also at stake in the way he treats the customer, but the distinctive breach he chose is the faking. Pride is moral ambition, not a talent for pretense. Politeness does not license the lie.

exercises.prompt: Which pair keeps both honesty and justice intact?

choices.text: She states the facts she chooses to state without faking, and she praises only the work that was done
He announces every passing thought, and he gives the same prize to every person
She hides a fraud behind a true detail, and she calls the hiding mercy
He never judges anyone, and he calls the refusal honesty

feedback.note: Honesty is kept when one does not fake, not when one publishes every thought. Justice is kept when praise matches the work, not when prizes are equal by policy. Hiding a fraud behind a true detail is still faking, and calling it mercy does not make it justice. Refusing to judge people abandons justice. It does not fulfill honesty, because honesty is not a ban on evaluation.

exercises.prompt: What is productiveness, as a virtue in this code?

choices.text: Motion with no product, so long as one stays busy
Seizing values other people have already created
Creating the values one's life requires, by shaping reality to a purpose
A job title, whether or not any value is produced

feedback.note: Productiveness is the virtue of creating values by thought and effort, because that is the process by which one's mind sustains one's life. Busyness with no product does not do it, and a title does not do it if nothing is created. Seizing other people's product is the opposite policy. The virtue is making, in service of a purpose, not appearing occupied.

exercises.prompt: What is pride, as one virtue in this code?

choices.text: Moral ambition: the commitment to earn the right to regard oneself as worthy of living
A demand that others admire one, whether or not anything was earned
A title inherited, with no further achievement required
Boasting, used as a substitute for the virtues

feedback.note: Pride is moral ambitiousness, because one holds oneself as one's highest value and, like every value, that estimate has to be earned. Vanity demands admiration one has not earned. A title and a boast do not earn it either. Pride is the policy of becoming worthy, not a claim on an audience and not a decoration placed on an empty record.

exercises.prompt: Match each policy to the virtue or the failure it is.

pairs.left: Shape reality so that it yields the values one's life requires
Earn the character that makes one worthy of that life
Live off values one did not create, and demand to feel worthy anyway

feedback.note: Productiveness supplies the values, and pride is the ambition to be worthy of the life those values make possible. Living off others while demanding an unearned estimate is neither, because nothing was created and nothing was earned. The two virtues support each other. They are not a pose on one side and a seizure on the other.

exercises.prompt: Complete the names of these two virtues.

parts.text: The virtue of making values is
, and the virtue of earning one's worth is

feedback.note: Productiveness names the making, and pride names the moral ambition, because one creates the values a life requires and the other commits one to being worthy of that life. Vanity and seizure are the failures: unearned admiration, and taking what one did not make. Neither word belongs in the pair of virtues.

exercises.prompt: An engineer builds a tool others freely buy, and he respects himself because the work and his judgment are real. Which pairing is this?

choices.text: Seizure plus vanity
Productiveness without any estimate of himself, which is the whole of pride
Pride with no product, which is enough
Productiveness and pride together

feedback.note: The work is productiveness, and the earned respect is pride, because he created a value and his estimate of himself tracks that fact. Seizure and vanity are the opposites. Pride is not the absence of an estimate, and a product is not dispensable. The pairing is the point of these two virtues: making values, and being worthy of the life they sustain.

exercises.prompt: A man produces real work and regards himself as rotten for having done it. What is present, and what is missing?

choices.text: Pride is present, and productiveness is missing
Productiveness is present, and pride is missing
Both are present, because self-contempt is moral ambition
Neither, because real work counts only if a crowd feels moved

feedback.note: The work is productiveness. The standing self-contempt is not pride, because pride is the commitment to regard oneself as worthy on the strength of what one has earned. Self-contempt rejects that ambition. A crowd's feeling is not what makes the work real. He has one virtue and is refusing the other.

exercises.prompt: A woman does no productive work, boasts of her superiority, and calls the boast pride. What is the right name?

choices.text: Vanity. Pride has to be earned, and there is no virtue here to have earned it
Pride, because a boast is the same act as moral ambition
Productiveness, because superiority is a product
Justice, because other people owe her the admiration

feedback.note: The boast is vanity, because pride is earned by the virtues, including productiveness, and she has not practiced them. A claim of superiority is not a product. Other people do not owe her admiration she has not earned. That demand fails justice as well, but the virtue she misnamed is pride. Moral ambition builds the worth. It does not announce a worth that was never made.

exercises.prompt: Why do productiveness and pride belong together at the end of the code?

choices.text: Because they replace rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, and justice
Because making values is a license to fake reality, and pride is a license to seize
Because one creates the values a rational life requires, and the other is the ambition to be worthy of that life
Because a busy pose and a boast are the practical form of the cardinal values

feedback.note: They belong together because productiveness is how one sustains one's life and pride is the moral ambition to be worthy of it. They do not replace the earlier virtues. Rationality remains primary, and faking or seizing would breach honesty, justice, and productiveness itself. A pose and a boast are the counterfeits. The code ends on making values and earning the character that can live by them.

exercises.prompt: What is morality, for a being who has to choose how to live?

choices.text: A code of values that guides the choices and actions a life depends on
A mood of approval that needs no stated values
A slogan repeated in place of a decision
A set of commands with no tie to what keeps a person alive

feedback.note: Morality is a code of values because the choices that shape a life need a guide, not a feeling standing in for one. A mood cannot do that work, because it reports an estimate and does not state what to pursue or refuse. Commands with no tie to life, and slogans, leave the choice without a standard.

exercises.prompt: A man must decide whether to learn a skill his work requires. What does a code of values do there?

choices.text: It waits until a mood is strong enough to replace the decision
It tells him to judge the skill by what his life requires, then act
It sets the decision outside morality because the skill is practical
It copies the oldest custom, whether or not the custom serves life

feedback.note: A code guides this choice by naming the skill as a value or not, according to what his life requires. Leaving practical choices outside morality treats a code as if it had nothing to say about the actions that sustain a person. A mood or an old custom does not supply that measure, because neither asks what the life requires.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it can actually play in a choice.

pairs.left: A code of values
pairs.right: A guide for what to pursue and what to refuse

pairs.left: A mood
pairs.right: A reaction that does not itself state the next action

pairs.left: A slogan
pairs.right: Words that supply no standard for action

pairs.left: A command cut off from life
pairs.right: An order with nothing that can measure it

feedback.note: Only a code of values can guide a choice, because it states what to pursue and what to refuse. A mood, a slogan, and a command cut off from life are the usual substitutes, and each fails for a different reason: one is only a reaction, one is only words, and one has no tie to the life the choice affects.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that states what morality is.

parts.text: Morality is a
of
that guides the choices a life depends on.

feedback.note: The principle names a code of values because morality has to guide choices, not decorate them. Calling it a mood or a slogan drops the guide and leaves the person with a reaction or a phrase. An omen is a different error, because it treats a sign as a substitute for judging what life requires.

exercises.prompt: Which question is a code of values supposed to answer?

choices.text: Which feeling is strongest in this hour?
Which phrase will draw the most applause?
Which actions sustain my life, and which work against it?
Which order can be obeyed with no reference to life at all?

feedback.note: A code of values answers which actions sustain a life and which work against it, because that is what a choosing being has to know. Applause and the strongest feeling are subjective substitutes, and they do not identify what the life requires. An order with no reference to life is a command, not a code of values.

exercises.prompt: A lecturer says moral rules bind whether or not they serve anyone's life. What is the error?

choices.text: He cuts the rules off from the life a code exists to guide
He is right, because a duty needs no connection to the person who must live
He is right, because morality is only a social ornament
The error is the idea that a code could guide a choice at all

feedback.note: The error is a duty with no tie to life: a code exists to guide the choices that sustain a person, so a rule that ignores that function is not a morality of values. The lecturer treats obedience as self-justifying, which is the Kantian split between duty and the needs of life. An ornament is a different mistake, and so is denying that a code can guide action.

exercises.prompt: Someone feels admiration for courage but, in action, always takes the easiest path. What is missing?

choices.text: A louder feeling of admiration
A slogan to replace the feeling
Nothing, because a feeling of admiration is already a code of values
A code that directs action, rather than a feeling that leaves action unguided

feedback.note: A feeling of admiration is not a code, because it does not direct the next action when ease pulls the other way. What is missing is a code of values that can guide the choice. Treating the feeling as already moral confuses an emotion with a standard, and a slogan would only rename the gap.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that states what morality is and what it is for.

tokens.text: a command with no tie to life

feedback.note: Morality is a code of values that guides the choices a life depends on. Calling it a social ornament treats a requirement as decoration. Calling it a command with no tie to life leaves a set of orders that cannot tell a person which actions sustain him, because they are cut off from the life the code is for.

exercises.prompt: Why does a human being need a code of values, when a plant does not?

choices.text: Because a human being already has an automatic code that selects every action
Because his consciousness is volitional, so he must choose and has no automatic code
Because society enjoys codes, whether or not any life depends on them
Because commands are binding only when they have no tie to life

feedback.note: Man needs a code because he is a being of volitional consciousness and has no automatic code of values. A plant acts by its nature without choosing a policy. The social-decoration answer and the baseless-command answer both drop that fact, because they give morality a source other than the kind of being he is.

exercises.prompt: A sparrow builds a nest by its nature, without a chosen policy. What follows for ethics?

choices.text: An automatic life does not need a moral code; a choosing life does
The sparrow is practicing the same morality a person must invent
Human beings also survive by an unchosen program, so no code is required
Ethics applies only to plants, because their action is automatic

feedback.note: Where action is automatic, no chosen code is required, because the organism does not select among policies. A human being does select, and he has no innate program that already ranks his values. Treating people as if they had that program denies volition. Treating the sparrow as a moral agent confuses automatic action with choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of life to what it does and does not need.

pairs.left: A plant's life
pairs.right: Automatic action, with no chosen code of values

pairs.left: A human life
pairs.right: Chosen action, which needs a code of values

pairs.left: A command with no tie to life
pairs.right: Not a substitute for the code a choosing mind needs

feedback.note: A plant does not choose, so it does not need a moral code. A human being does choose, because his consciousness is volitional, and a code is what guides those choices. A command with no tie to life does not fill that need, because it is not derived from what his life requires.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reason a human being needs a moral code.

parts.text: Man's consciousness is volitional, so the actions that sustain his life must be

feedback.note: The actions have to be chosen because a volitional consciousness has no automatic code of values. Calling them automatic or inherited treats man as if he were a plant or a finished program. Calling them revealed swaps a command for the judgment he still has to make, and that command need not have any tie to his life.

exercises.prompt: Someone says instinct already ranks every human value, so a moral code is a luxury. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, because instinct is a code of values a person chooses
The error is admitting that human beings act at all
Man has no such instinct. He must choose, and a code is what guides the choice
The error is thinking that only human beings are alive

feedback.note: There is no automatic human code that already ranks values, because man is a being of volitional consciousness. Calling morality a luxury treats a requirement of that fact as an extra. Instinct would fit a life that does not choose. It does not fit a life that has to select its actions.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the consciousness that makes a moral code necessary?
exercises.quote: The key to what you so recklessly call "human nature," the open secret you live with, yet dread to name, is the fact that man is a being of volitional consciousness.

choices.text: Man's consciousness is automatic and already contains a code of values
Man is a being of volitional consciousness, so his mind does not run by itself
Volition belongs to plants, and human action is an unchosen reflex
A moral code is a social ornament added after survival is guaranteed

feedback.quote: The key to what you so recklessly call "human nature," the open secret you live with, yet dread to name, is the fact that man is a being of volitional consciousness.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 120
feedback.note: The passage establishes that man is a being of volitional consciousness. That is why he has no automatic code of values and must choose the actions that sustain his life. The instinct reading denies the passage, because it treats his consciousness as a program that already knows what to do. An ornament is not what this fact requires.

exercises.prompt: A person says, "I have a mind, so the right action will occur without a policy." What does he miss?

choices.text: That a mind cancels the need to choose
That the right action is whatever feels easiest
That a policy is useful only as a social ornament
That a volitional mind does not act rightly unless he chooses to think and has a code

feedback.note: Having a mind does not make the right action automatic, because the choice to think is volitional and values are not innate. He still needs a code to guide the choices that sustain his life. Ease is a whim, and an ornament is a decoration, and neither is the policy a choosing mind requires.

exercises.prompt: Which claim keeps the reason morality is required?

choices.text: A choosing being, with no automatic code, needs a guide for the actions his life depends on
Morality is required only as a courtesy once food and work are already secure
Morality is required because a group prefers ceremonies
Morality is required as a list of orders that ignore what life needs

feedback.note: Morality is required because man must choose and has no automatic code of values to do the choosing for him. Ceremony and courtesy treat that need as decoration. Orders that ignore what life needs are commands with no tie to the life the code is supposed to sustain, so they are not the reason either.

exercises.prompt: Why is morality not a decoration added once life is already secure?

choices.text: Because decoration is the only form a code of values can take
Because a life can be secured by any means, and a code is paint added later
Because the choices that secure a life are already the choices a code must guide
Because morality binds only when it has no connection to survival

feedback.note: The choices that secure a life are moral choices, because they are the actions a code of values exists to guide. Treating morality as paint added later pretends those actions can be chosen with no standard. A command with no connection to survival is a further error, since it also cuts the code off from life.

exercises.prompt: A man says he will get money by any means now and adopt a moral code later, if he wants an ornament. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, if the ornament is expensive enough
The means are choices that need a standard now. A code is not an ornament added after
The error is wanting the money his life may require
He should obey a command that has no tie to life and call that step practical

feedback.note: Every means is already a choice, so it needs a code now, because "any means" includes actions that can destroy the life he claims to secure. Calling the code an ornament postpones the standard until after the choices that matter. Wanting the money is not the error. A baseless command would not make the means practical.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to what it says morality is.

pairs.left: An ornament added after survival
pairs.right: A decoration, not a requirement of life

pairs.left: A luxury one can skip and still live as a choosing being
A guide for the choices life depends on
pairs.right: The requirement a volitional being has

pairs.left: Orders that ignore what life needs
pairs.right: Commands with no tie to life

feedback.note: Morality is the guide a volitional being needs, because his choices have no automatic code behind them. An ornament, a luxury, and a set of life-ignoring orders all treat that guide as something other than a requirement. The luxury claim is the same error as the ornament, dressed as a budget. The orders are the error of duty with no tie to life.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between a requirement and an ornament.

parts.text: Treating a code as an optional social extra makes morality a

feedback.note: Decoration names the error, because an optional social extra is an ornament, not the code a life requires. Foundation, premise, and cause are names for something morality can rest on or be, so they do not name the error. The point is that a requirement of life is not jewelry added after survival.

exercises.prompt: Someone calls honesty a luxury to add after he is rich, and calls fraud practical until then. Which error is this?

choices.text: He treats a virtue his life requires as an ornament, and fraud as a neutral tool
He treats fraud as a command with no tie to life, and rejects it for that reason
He is right, because wealth is outside the choices a code can guide
He is right, because a code applies only to people who are already safe

feedback.note: Honesty is not a luxury, because faking reality is a way of acting, and the means of getting rich are choices a code must judge. Calling fraud practical treats morality as decoration added after the loot is in. Safety does not come first and morality second. The actions that seek safety are already under the code.

exercises.prompt: A host says morality is etiquette: useful at a table, irrelevant to work, money, and survival. What has he done?

choices.text: He has stated the reason a choosing being needs a code
He has tied every rule to what a human life requires
He has shown that plants need etiquette too
He has reduced a code of values to a social ornament

feedback.note: Etiquette at a table is a social form. Morality is a code for the choices that sustain a life, including work and money, so shrinking it to table manners makes it a decoration. The reduction fails because those practical choices are exactly what a volitional being cannot leave to whim or to an unchosen habit.

exercises.prompt: A person already fed and employed says he is past the need for a code. What does he overlook?

choices.text: That a code is needed only by people who are hungry
That employment cancels volition
That staying alive as a rational being is an ongoing set of choices, not a finished ornament
That a command with no tie to life becomes necessary only after one is safe

feedback.note: Food and a job are results of choices, and keeping a life is a further series of choices, so a code remains a requirement rather than a prize for people still in trouble. Volition does not switch off when a person is fed. A baseless command is not what safety adds. The code guides the life he is still living.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim that morality is required rather than added afterward.

tokens.text: a command with no tie to life

feedback.note: A code guides the choices that sustain life, so it is not an ornament added once someone feels safe. "Optional once one feels safe" is the decoration error, because the choices that keep a life are still open. A command with no tie to life is a different substitute, and it does not state what the code is for.

exercises.prompt: What happens to choices when a person has no code of values?

choices.text: They have no standard, so action drifts by whim and is not a policy for living
They become automatically right, because a code would only interfere
They are settled by whatever command ignores life most completely
They remain a policy, because a whim is a standard under another name

feedback.note: Without a code there is no standard, so choices drift by whim, and a whim is not a policy that can sustain a life. Calling the drift automatically right pretends an absent code is a success. A command that ignores life does not replace a standard, because it still does not say what the life requires. Subjectivism errs by promoting the whim into the standard it cannot be.

exercises.prompt: A student picks a career by this morning's mood and expects to reverse it tonight. What is he using in place of a code?

choices.text: A long-range standard tied to the life he is trying to live
A policy that ranks the work by what a rational life requires
A whim, which sets no standard he can still accept tomorrow
An automatic instinct that already chose the right career

feedback.note: A mood he plans to reverse is a whim, because it does not state a value he is acting to keep. A code would rank the work by what his life requires and would not expire at night. Instinct is the wrong substitute here, since a human being has no automatic career program. The mood feels like a decision and is not a policy.

exercises.prompt: Match each guide to what it can and cannot do.

pairs.left: A code of values
pairs.right: A policy one can apply to the next choice

pairs.left: A whim
pairs.right: A feeling with no standard one is committed to keep

pairs.left: One lucky result
pairs.right: Not a policy, even if a single action turned out well

feedback.note: A code is a policy because it can be applied again, to the next choice, by the same standard. A whim cannot, because nothing in it commits the person to a value once the feeling changes. One lucky result does not convert either gap into a policy. Chance is not a code.

exercises.prompt: Complete the description of action that has no code behind it.

parts.text: With no code of values, choice drifts by
, and a whim is not a policy for living.

feedback.note: Whim is what remains when a code is absent, because nothing else is setting a standard the person means to keep. Reason, principle, and judgment are what a code puts to work, so they do not name the drift. The point is that a changing feeling is not a policy capable of guiding a life.

exercises.prompt: A subjectivist says the whim is the standard, so nothing is missing when there is no code. What is the mistake?

choices.text: He is right, because a feeling is the same fact as a code of values
A whim cannot guide the range of choices a life requires. Naming it a standard does not make it one
The mistake is wanting any standard at all
The mistake is refusing a supernatural command

feedback.note: Subjectivism treats a feeling as if it were a standard. It is not, because a whim does not identify what sustains a life across the choices a person must make. Renaming it a code does not give it that power. The error is not the desire for a standard, and it is not the refusal of a command that has no tie to life.

exercises.prompt: A gambler says he needs no code because one reckless bet once paid. What does that result not show?

choices.text: That a single win is a code of values
That recklessness is a policy a life can be built on
That chance has the same role as a chosen standard
That a lucky result can replace a policy for the choices still to come

feedback.note: One payment does not show that recklessness is a policy, because a life is a long run of choices and chance does not rank them. A code would tell him which risks serve his life and which throw it away. Treating the win as a standard confuses a result with a principle he can apply again.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "I care about my life, so I do not need a code." What is still missing?

choices.text: A standard that can tell a particular choice whether it serves that life or works against it
A stronger wish, since caring is already a full policy
Permission from a crowd to care
A command that does not consult his life at all

feedback.note: Caring names a concern, not a guide, because it does not yet say which action serves the life and which destroys it. That is what a code of values is for. A stronger wish is still a whim. A crowd's permission and a life-ignoring command both hand the standard to something other than the life he says he cares about.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim about choice when no code is present.

feedback.note: Without a code, choices have no standard and drift by whim, which is not a policy for living. "An automatic success" pretends the drift is safe. "A revealed command" offers orders in place of a standard tied to life. Neither gives the person a policy he can use, because neither identifies what his life requires.

exercises.prompt: Which statement holds the full reason man needs morality?

choices.text: Man needs a slogan, because a plant is volitional and a code is a decoration
Man needs a code of values because he must choose, has no automatic code, and his life depends on those choices
Man needs commands with no tie to life, because whim is already a policy
Man needs morality only after survival is finished, as a social ornament

feedback.note: The full reason joins three facts: he must choose, he has no automatic code of values, and the choices decide whether he lives. A slogan, a decoration, and a set of baseless commands each drop part of that reason. Whim is not already a policy. The need is not something to add once life is over, because the choices are what the life depends on.

exercises.prompt: A promoter says, "Cheat now, get rich, and wear a moral code later as jewelry." Which parts of the reason does he drop?

choices.text: That the means are choices needing a standard now, and that a code is not jewelry
Only the jewelry, because cheating is outside choice
Nothing, if the jewelry is added before he spends the money
That plants also need jewelry in order to grow

feedback.note: Cheating is a choice, so it needs a code now, and calling the code jewelry is the decoration error. Both parts fall together: without a standard the means drift by whim, and a whim is not a policy for the life he says the money will serve. Waiting until the money is spent does not put the standard back in front of the choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each error to the part of the reason it drops.

pairs.left: Morality is a mood
pairs.right: Drops the code that guides choices

pairs.left: Instinct already ranks human values
pairs.right: Drops volition and the lack of an automatic code

pairs.left: A code is jewelry for after one is safe
pairs.right: Drops the fact that the need is not decorative

pairs.left: A whim is a good enough policy
pairs.right: Drops the need for a standard

feedback.note: Each error removes a different part of one reason. A mood is not a code. Instinct denies that man must choose. Jewelry treats a requirement as decoration. A whim is what action becomes when the standard is gone. Keeping the reason means refusing all four, because each one leaves the choices of a life unguided.

exercises.prompt: Build the full reason morality is required.

tokens.text: and those choices sustain his life

feedback.note: Man needs a code of values because he must choose, he has no automatic code, and the choices are what sustain his life. "As a social ornament" turns the need into decoration. "By whim alone" pretends the absence of a standard is a method. Both contradict the reason, because a volitional being cannot live by an unchosen program or by a changing feeling.

exercises.prompt: A mystic says a voice issues orders, you need not ask what they do to your life, and the orders are your morality. What is this?

choices.text: A code of values derived from what a choosing being requires
A recognition that man has no automatic code and must judge by his life
Commands with no tie to life, offered in place of a code of values
A policy that keeps whim from running the choices

feedback.note: Orders one must not test against life are commands with no tie to life, not a code of values, because a code exists to guide the choices that sustain a volitional being. Refusing that test leaves him with someone else's orders or with whim. Neither is the morality his kind of consciousness requires, since neither is drawn from what his life needs.

exercises.prompt: Someone argues that animals flourish without ethics, so ethics is an optional human ornament. What is the reply?

choices.text: Animals are volitional, so their flourishing proves a code is optional for man too
Man flourishes by the same automatic action, so a code would be pretence
The reply is that ornaments are what keep animals alive
Animals act automatically. Man does not, so a code is a requirement of his consciousness, not an ornament

feedback.note: The animal case shows why a code is not universal furniture. It does not show that man can skip one, because his consciousness is volitional and theirs is not. Calling ethics an ornament imports the decoration error into a contrast that actually explains the need. Automatic action is not available to him as a substitute.

exercises.prompt: A woman states a code every morning and suspends it whenever it would change what she does. What is she living by?

choices.text: A code of values, because the morning statement is enough
Whim, with a code's name and none of a code's guidance
An automatic instinct that matches the stated code
A requirement of life, because suspension proves she is choosing

feedback.note: A code guides action. A statement she drops whenever it binds does not, so the action is whim wearing a moral label. Choice is real here, and that is why she needs a code she will actually use. Instinct is not what is suspending the rule. The morning recital is decoration if it never directs a choice.

exercises.prompt: A reformer offers a code that praises actions he admits will destroy the agent's life. Can it be the morality a choosing being needs?

choices.text: No. A code of values has to guide the choices that sustain life, not a policy of destroying it
Yes, because a code is nobler when it has no tie to life
Yes, if the destruction is called a social ornament
Yes, because any stated list is a policy for living

feedback.note: The morality a volitional being needs is a code for the choices his life depends on. A list that directs him to destroy that life is not that code, however formally it is stated. "No tie to life" is the error of baseless command, and calling the destruction an ornament does not repair it. A policy for living cannot be a policy for ending the life.

exercises.prompt: What does a trader do in an exchange with another person?

choices.text: He gives a value and receives a value, by the judgment of each party
He receives a value and gives nothing, if his need is sincere
He gives a value only when a duty says he must come out behind
He exchanges cash only, and personal relationships are outside the principle

feedback.note: A trader gives value for value, because each party offers something the other judges worth receiving. Need does not entitle him to a one-sided receipt, and a duty to come out behind is a sacrifice, not a trade. The principle is not confined to cash. Friendship, praise, and work are exchanges of value too, when each side is offering something real.

exercises.prompt: An editor pays a writer the price they both accepted, and the writer delivers the piece they described. What kind of exchange is this?

choices.text: A seizure, because money changed hands
A sacrifice by the editor, because he no longer has the fee
A trade: each gave a value and received a value
A gift the writer was owed whether or not he wrote

feedback.note: It is a trade, because the fee and the piece are values each party chose to exchange. The editor's payment is not a sacrifice if he values the piece more than the fee, and the writer's work is not a seizure of the editor. The writer was not owed the fee for a piece he might never deliver. Value for value is what both of them practiced.

exercises.prompt: Match each exchange to the pattern it follows.

pairs.left: Work given for an agreed payment
Loyalty given for loyalty between friends
pairs.right: Value for value, and not only in cash

pairs.left: A product demanded because the demander needs it

feedback.note: Value for value covers material and personal exchanges, because a value need not be cash to be something one acts to gain or keep. Work for pay is the plain case. Loyalty for loyalty is the same pattern between people who are values to each other. A demand from need, with nothing offered, drops the giving. It asks for the unearned.

exercises.prompt: Complete the trader rule of the exchange.

parts.text: A trader gives value for

feedback.note: Value completes the rule, because what he receives has to be a value, just as what he gives is a value. Need, pity, and force are substitutes that ask him to give without receiving, or to receive without the other party's judgment. They turn the exchange into a demand. A trader does not deal on those terms.

exercises.prompt: Two friends spend time together because each judges the other's company worth more than the hour. Is this outside the trader principle?

choices.text: Yes, because the principle applies only to invoices
No. Each is giving a value and receiving a value, by his own judgment
Yes, because friendship is a duty to come out behind
No, only if one of them is paying the other a wage

feedback.note: It is inside the principle, because each friend offers his company as a value and receives the other's, and both judge the exchange worth making. Invoices are not the boundary. A duty to lose would make the hour a sacrifice, which neither of them is performing. A wage is one form of value, not the only form. The pattern is the same wherever a value is traded for a value.

exercises.prompt: A client wants the writer's week and offers nothing the writer values, then calls the request a trade. What is missing?

choices.text: Nothing, if the client uses the word trade
A duty for the writer to accept, which would create the value
Force, which is what turns a request into value for value
A value given in return, which the writer can judge worth receiving

feedback.note: The value in return is missing, because a trade is not the word trade attached to a one-sided demand. A duty to accept would make the week a sacrifice, not a trade. Force would make it a seizure. The writer has to receive something he judges to be a value, just as the client hopes to receive the work. Without that, nothing is being exchanged.

exercises.prompt: Which formula states the principle without shrinking it to cash or swelling it into a duty?

choices.text: Give a value and receive a value, in work, money, or a personal bond
Give cash and ignore every other kind of value
Give whatever is demanded, and count the loss as the value received
Receive whatever you need, and call the need the value you gave

feedback.note: The principle is value for value across the kinds of value people actually exchange, because a personal bond can be a value and a loss is not a value received. Shrinking it to cash drops half of human trade. Counting a loss as the thing received is a sacrifice. Counting a need as something one gave pretends that wanting is producing. None of those is the trader's rule.

exercises.prompt: Build the trader rule in the order that keeps it.

feedback.note: A trader gives value for value. Need is not a value given, and a duty to lose is a sacrifice, because both ask one party to hand over a good with nothing he judges worth receiving. The rule is an exchange, judged by each side, not a claim and not a surrender. It holds for personal values as well as for money.

exercises.prompt: Why can both parties gain in one and the same trade?

choices.text: Because they receive the same object in the same amount
Because each values what he receives more than what he gives, by his own judgment
Because one must lose, and the loss is renamed a gain
Because a third party forces the terms and calls the force mutual

feedback.note: Both gain because each judges the good he receives as worth more to him than the good he gives. They need not receive the same object or the same amount. Renaming a loss as a gain is a sacrifice pretending to be a trade. Force removes the judgment. A trade is voluntary, and the gain on each side is real to the person who chose it.

exercises.prompt: A baker trades bread for a mechanic's repair. Each prefers what he receives. A bystander says one of them must have lost, or it was not an exchange. What is the error?

choices.text: He treats gain as a single sum that cannot rise for both, which a trade does not require
He is right, because preference is not a way of gaining
He is right, because bread and repair are the same object
The error is allowing either of them to prefer anything
