feedback.note: The error is a zero-sum picture, because each man's gain is measured by his own values, not by a single pile that one must shrink for the other to grow. Preference is exactly how each judges that he gained. The goods are not the same object, which is why the trade has a point. Forbidding preference would forbid the judgment a trade depends on.

exercises.prompt: Match each picture of an exchange to what it claims.

pairs.left: Each prefers what he receives
One man's gain is the other man's loss, as a rule
pairs.right: A zero-sum picture, not a trade

pairs.left: The terms are forced, and the victim is told he gained

feedback.note: Both gain when each prefers what he receives, because the values are ranked by the people in the exchange. A standing rule that one must lose denies that possibility. Force, followed by a speech about the victim's gain, is not a judgment he made. It is a seizure described in the language of trade. The description does not create the gain.

exercises.prompt: Complete what each party uses to judge his gain.

parts.text: Each party gains by his own
, not by being forced and not by losing on purpose.

feedback.note: Judgment is what each party uses, because he has to decide that what he receives is worth more to him than what he gives. Loss, fear, and duty are ways of arranging for him not to gain, or not to choose. They do not name the measure of a trade. A trade in which one side is required to lose is no longer a trade for both.

exercises.prompt: The baker would rather keep his bread than accept a repair he does not need, and he says so. Has a trade occurred?

choices.text: Yes, because the mechanic wanted the bread
Yes, because refusing is a way of gaining the repair
Yes, if a bystander declares that both gained
No. His judgment is that he would not gain, so there is no exchange

feedback.note: No trade occurred, because he does not value the repair more than the bread, and his judgment is the one that would have to find a gain. The mechanic's desire is only one side. A bystander cannot declare the gain into existence. Refusal is not a hidden acceptance. Both-gain requires two judgments, and one of them is missing.

exercises.prompt: A contract is signed because each side expects to gain, and later one side dislikes the bargain he understood. What does the dislike not show?

choices.text: That he may not regret a term he actually accepted
That new facts can matter to what he does next
That the original exchange was a loss merely because he no longer likes it
That force and trade are different

feedback.note: The later dislike does not show that he lost in the exchange he judged at the time, because a gain is fixed by the judgment that made the trade, not by a mood after it. He may still regret a term, and new facts can change his next choice. Force remains different from trade. The error is rewriting the past judgment as if a feeling could cancel the value he received.

exercises.prompt: Which exchange is one in which both sides gain?

choices.text: A thief takes the bread and leaves the baker a lecture about sharing
Each agrees, and each would rather have what he receives than what he gives
One signs because he was threatened, and the other is pleased
Both are ordered to exchange goods neither wants, for the sake of a plan

feedback.note: Only the agreed exchange, with each preferring what he receives, is a gain for both, because each judgment finds a value. The lecture is not a value the baker chose. A threat removes one judgment. An order that neither wants is a double loss described as a plan. Pleasure on one side is not enough. Both sides have to gain by standards they accept.

exercises.prompt: Build the reason both sides can gain from one trade.

feedback.note: Each values what he receives more than what he gives. "Must lose" is the zero-sum claim, and "is forced" removes the judgment, because a trade's gain exists only in the values of the people who chose it. They do not need identical goods. They need two real preferences, each counting the receipt as the better side of the exchange.

exercises.prompt: What is the unearned, in the trader's rule?

choices.text: A value one seeks, or grants as a duty, without a value given in return
Any gift to a person one values, scaled to that person's place in one's life
The payment received for work one actually did
A wage both parties judged and agreed to

feedback.note: The unearned is a value sought or granted with nothing given in return, because a trader does not seek it and does not grant it as if desert were irrelevant. A gift to someone who is a value in one's life, at the rank that person holds, is not that demand. Pay for work done, and a wage both sides judged, are values exchanged. They are the earned, which is what the rule protects.

exercises.prompt: An employee asks for a bonus for a project he did not do, and he calls the bonus fair because he wants it. What is he seeking?

choices.text: A value for a value, because the want is the value he gave
Justice, because desire and desert are the same fact
The unearned, a reward with no value given in return
A trade, because the employer still has money

feedback.note: He is seeking the unearned, because no value was given for the bonus. A want is not a value produced. Desire is not desert, so the request is not justice. The employer's money is not a standing offer. A trader does not seek a reward for a default, and he does not treat another person's product as available on the ground that he wishes it were.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to the thing it is actually asking for.

pairs.left: Pay me for the work I did
Praise me for a virtue I have not practiced
I give this to her because she is a great value in my life
pairs.right: Not a demand for the unearned

pairs.left: Love me as a duty, though you do not value me

feedback.note: Pay for work done is value for value. Praise for an absent virtue, and love demanded from someone who does not value you, seek the unearned in spirit, because desert is being bypassed. A gift to a person who holds a real place in one's life expresses that value. It is not a duty to hand the same gift to a stranger, and it is not a claim the stranger can make.

exercises.prompt: Complete both directions of the trader rule.

parts.text: A trader does not seek or grant the

feedback.note: Unearned is what he refuses in both directions, because seeking it asks for a value he did not produce, and granting it as a duty treats desert as irrelevant. Payment, product, and agreement are the stuff of an actual trade. They do not name the thing the rule forbids. The refusal covers matter and spirit: money, praise, and love.

exercises.prompt: A woman supports a friend's first show because the friend's work and character are values to her, and the sum fits that rank. A stranger then demands the same sum as a right. Which request seeks the unearned?

choices.text: The woman's gift, because all gifts are unearned by definition
Neither, because a demand and a chosen gift are the same act
The woman's gift, because the friend benefits
The stranger's demand. The gift was an expression of a value. The demand is a claim with nothing offered

feedback.note: The stranger seeks the unearned, because nothing in his demand is a value given, and the woman's hierarchy does not include him at that rank. Her gift is not a definition of the unearned. It is a value she chose to give a person who had earned that place with her. His benefit is not what makes her act a seizure of herself. The right he asserts is the thing the trader refuses to grant.

exercises.prompt: Why does the rule forbid granting the unearned, and not only seeking it?

choices.text: Because a trader should never give anything to anyone he values
Because granting the undeserved, as a duty, treats people without regard to the facts
Because every receipt is unearned if the receiver is glad
Because justice is a ban on exchange

feedback.note: Granting is included because handing out the undeserved as a duty is the other half of refusing to judge people by what they have done. It is not a ban on giving to someone one values, and it is not a claim that gladness makes a receipt unearned. Justice is the virtue that matches treatment to desert. A ban on exchange would be the opposite of the trader's rule, which exists so that earned values can change hands.

exercises.prompt: Which request may a trader grant without breaking the rule?

choices.text: A price for goods delivered, at terms he judges worth accepting
A prize for a failure, demanded as his moral debt
Admiration for a record he knows is faked
Love, claimed by a person he does not value, as an obligation

feedback.note: The price for goods delivered is earned, because a value was given and he judges the terms. A prize for failure, admiration for a fake, and love as an obligation are grants of the unearned, in money or in spirit. Gladness on the asker's side does not create the missing value. A trader can be generous toward people who are values to him. He does not owe a counterfeit the same treatment.

exercises.prompt: Build the negative half of the trader's rule.

tokens.text: a gift to someone you value

feedback.note: Do not seek or grant the unearned. Payment for work done is the earned, and a gift to someone you value, inside your hierarchy, is not the thing forbidden, because that person has a place your judgment assigned. The rule covers both directions and both matter and spirit. It does not turn every receipt into a crime and every gift into a duty.

exercises.prompt: How does a trade differ from taking another person's value?

choices.text: It does not. Taking is a trade the other party has not noticed
A trade is any transfer, including one produced by a threat
A trade is an agreed exchange of value for value. Taking seizes a value
A trade is worse than taking, because both parties consent

feedback.note: A trade is an agreed exchange of value for value, and taking seizes a value without that exchange, because the victim's judgment is bypassed. An unnoticed theft is not a subtle trade. A threat does not become an agreement by being called a transfer. Consent is not a defect. It is what makes the gain mutual rather than a one-sided extraction.

exercises.prompt: A buyer pays for a shipment that the seller never had. The seller keeps the money. What is this, if not a trade?

choices.text: A fake of trade. Payment was taken for a value that was not given
A trade, because money moved
A gift the buyer chose, since he wanted the goods
Justice, because the seller desired the money

feedback.note: It is fraud, a form of taking, because the payment does not match a value given. Money moving is not enough to make a trade. The buyer's desire for the goods was the reason he paid, not a decision to donate. The seller's desire is not desert. Value for value failed on the seller's side, and the failure is a seizure carried out with the paperwork of an exchange.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the name it deserves.

pairs.left: Goods delivered for an agreed price
Goods taken, with a threat in place of a price
A price kept, and the goods never delivered
pairs.right: Taking, by a fake of trade

pairs.left: "Give it to me because I need it"
pairs.right: A one-sided demand, not a trade

feedback.note: Delivery for an agreed price is value for value. A threat replaces the other party's judgment, so it is taking. A price for nothing is the same seizure in reverse, because the value that was supposed to be given is absent. Need, offered as the whole of the claim, is a demand for the unearned. None of the last three becomes a trade by using commercial words.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast the principle draws.

parts.text: Trade is an exchange. Taking is a

feedback.note: Seizure names taking, because the value moves without an exchange the other party judged. Judgment, payment, and agreement are parts of a trade, or of what makes one possible. They do not name the thing trade is being distinguished from. A payment extracted by a lie is still a seizure. The paper does not change the act.

exercises.prompt: A landlord says, "Sign, or I will harm you," and the tenant signs. The landlord calls the signature a trade. Why does the signature not make it one?

choices.text: It does make it one, because a signature is consent
It fails only if the rent is high. The threat is irrelevant
It is a trade if the tenant needed the apartment
The signature was produced by a threat, so his judgment did not set the terms

feedback.note: The signature does not make a trade, because a threat replaces the tenant's judgment with fear. Consent under that condition is not the agreement value for value requires. A high rent, by itself, would be a term he could refuse. Need does not turn a threat into an offer. The landlord took the signature. He did not trade for it.

exercises.prompt: Which payment matches a value that was actually given?

choices.text: A bonus for a default the contract did not reward
The agreed fee, paid when the work described was done
A bill for goods the seller decided not to send
A fine invented after the work, with no term the worker accepted

feedback.note: The agreed fee for work done matches a value given, because both the work and the fee were part of the exchange. A bonus for a default, a bill for nothing, and a fine never accepted are payments detached from a value the other party gave or from a term he judged. They are ways of taking. Matching is the difference between a trade and a seizure that keeps the vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: A neighbor borrows a tool and returns it with the repair he promised. Another neighbor takes the tool and calls the taking a loan. Where is the trade?

choices.text: Only in the first case, where a value was returned for the value borrowed
In both, because both neighbors ended up with the tool at some point
Only in the second, because taking is more efficient
In neither, because a tool cannot be a value

feedback.note: The trade is the first case, because the repair was the value given for the loan, and both people understood it. Possession at some point is not an exchange. Efficiency does not rename a seizure. A tool is a value to the person who uses it. The second neighbor took it. The word loan does not supply the return he never made.

exercises.prompt: Build the line between trade and taking.

feedback.note: Trade exchanges a value for a value by agreement. By threat, and for nothing, are the two forms of taking, because one replaces judgment with force and the other omits the value that was supposed to be given. A one-sided demand from need belongs with them. The commercial vocabulary does not move an act across the line.

exercises.prompt: Which statement holds both clauses, including when a case looks mixed?

choices.text: Give value for value, except when one would rather seize the unearned
Give value for value, and do not seek or grant the unearned
Do not trade, and do not let anyone earn a value either
Seek the unearned from strangers, and trade only with friends

feedback.note: Both clauses belong together, because giving value for value is how one deals, and refusing the unearned is how one keeps that dealing just. An exception for seizure cancels the second clause. A ban on earning cancels the first. Seeking the unearned from strangers, while reserving trade for friends, splits the rule by person. The rule is the same for both clauses and for every party.

exercises.prompt: Two builders compete for one contract. Each offers his own work, and the client picks one. Has a conflict of rational interests appeared?

choices.text: No. Neither desires the unearned, and the client is trading for a value
Yes, because only one can be paid, so one man's life requires the other's loss
Yes, unless the loser is paid for the work he did not do
No, only if the winner seizes the loser's tools as part of the prize

feedback.note: No conflict of rational interests appears, because each builder's interest is to produce and offer, not to be handed a contract he did not earn, and the client gives a value for the value he chooses. Only one payment is not a clash of interests among men who do not desire the unearned. Paying the loser for work he did not do would create the unearned. Seizing tools would be taking, which neither builder's interest includes.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the clause it meets or breaks.

pairs.left: A contract both sides chose, each giving a value
A bonus added for work nobody did
pairs.right: Breaks the refusal of the unearned

pairs.left: Two producers competing by the work they offer
A demand that the winner split the pay with anyone who wanted the job
pairs.right: A desire for the unearned, which does clash

feedback.note: The contract is value for value. The bonus seeks the unearned, even if it is stapled to a real contract, because the mixed case does not make the extra into a value given. Competition by production is not a conflict of rational interests. A forced split treats the desire to have been chosen as if it were work. That desire is the unearned, and it does clash with the winner's interest.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about rational interests and traders?
exercises.quote: It holds that the rational interests of men do not clash—that there is no conflict of interests among men who do not desire the unearned, who do not make sacrifices nor accept them, who deal with one another as traders, giving value for value.

choices.text: Any two desires clash, so trade is a polite form of sacrifice
Interests clash unless someone grants the unearned
Traders are people who seek the unearned and call the seeking a bargain
Rational interests do not clash among men who refuse the unearned and trade value for value

feedback.quote: It holds that the rational interests of men do not clash—that there is no conflict of interests among men who do not desire the unearned, who do not make sacrifices nor accept them, who deal with one another as traders, giving value for value.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 31
feedback.note: The passage establishes that rational interests do not clash among men who refuse the unearned, make no sacrifices, and trade value for value. Ordinary desires can differ. Granting the unearned does not prevent a clash, because that grant is what these men do not do. Sacrifice is likewise absent from their dealing.

exercises.prompt: Complete the condition under which rational interests do not clash.

parts.text: They do not clash among men who deal as traders and do not desire the

feedback.note: Unearned completes the condition, because the no-clash claim is about men who do not want a value they did not earn and who trade value for value. A contract, a product, and a payment are things those men may pursue by producing them. They are not the desire that would create a clash. Wanting the same earned reward, and competing for it, is not that desire.

exercises.prompt: A fair sale is agreed, and the seller then adds, "Also pay me for a second job I did not perform." Which clause, if either, breaks?

choices.text: The sale breaks, and the extra is fine
Both break, because any price is unearned
The sale can stand. The extra seeks the unearned
Neither breaks, because he used the word pay

feedback.note: The sale can be value for value while the extra seeks the unearned, because a mixed case has to be split. Calling every price unearned would erase the first clause. The word pay does not earn the second job. Rational interests are not in conflict inside the sale. They would be put in conflict by a demand that the buyer fund work that was never done.

exercises.prompt: A theorist says that if two rational people both want a result, one of them must be sacrificed or the world is unjust. What has he assumed?

choices.text: That traders give value for value and do not desire the unearned
That a desire for a result, even an unearned one, is a rational interest
That competition by production is a form of robbery
That both can gain only by receiving identical objects

feedback.note: He has assumed that wanting a result is already a rational interest, including when the result would be unearned, because that is the only way two such people are forced into a sacrifice. The trader's clauses deny the assumption. Competition by production is not robbery, and identical objects are not required for both to gain. The injustice would be the sacrifice he thinks the situation demands, not the refusal to make it.

exercises.prompt: Build the full rule a trader has to keep.

feedback.note: Give value for value, and do not seek or grant the unearned. Making a sacrifice and desiring a clash contradict the rule, because men who trade and refuse the unearned do not have conflicting rational interests. A mixed case is judged clause by clause. The earned exchange stays, and the unearned extra goes. Neither clause is a favor reserved for friends.

exercises.prompt: What does the word sacrifice name in this account?

choices.text: Giving up a greater value for a lesser one, or for something that is not a value
Giving up a lesser value for a greater one
Any cost, including a cost paid to gain something one values more
The rejection of something worthless in order to keep something precious

feedback.note: Sacrifice names the surrender of a greater value for a lesser one or for a nonvalue, because the rank is what makes the surrender a loss of what matters more. Trading up is not that act. A cost paid for a higher value is a gain. Rejecting the worthless for the precious is the opposite policy. The word is not a name for every loss, and it is not a compliment.

exercises.prompt: A man gives up a career he ranks as central in order to keep a comfort he ranks as trivial. What is the exchange?

choices.text: A gain, because he still has the comfort
Not a sacrifice, because the career was only a value
A sacrifice, because the greater value is surrendered for the lesser one
A trade up, because comfort is always the higher value

feedback.note: It is a sacrifice, because he surrenders what he himself ranks higher for what he ranks lower. Keeping the comfort does not make the exchange a gain. The career's being a value is the reason giving it up hurts the hierarchy, not a reason to deny the sacrifice. Comfort is not automatically higher. His ranking is the measure, and by that measure he moved down.

exercises.prompt: Match each exchange to the name that fits the ranks.

pairs.left: A greater value given up for a lesser one
A greater value given up for something one does not value at all
A lesser value given up for a greater one

feedback.note: The first two are sacrifices, because a greater value is surrendered, whether the thing accepted is a lesser value or no value. The third is a gain by one's own ranking. Calling it a sacrifice would make every rational choice a sacrifice, since every choice forgoes the alternative. The word is reserved for the downward trade.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the act that the word sacrifice names?
exercises.quote: "Sacrifice" is the surrender of a greater value for the sake of a lesser one or of a nonvalue.

choices.text: Any cost is a sacrifice, whatever one gains by paying it
Sacrifice is the surrender of a greater value for a lesser one or a nonvalue
Sacrifice is giving up the lesser for the greater
Sacrifice is exchanging something worthless for something precious

feedback.quote: "Sacrifice" is the surrender of a greater value for the sake of a lesser one or of a nonvalue.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Ethics of Emergencies," The Virtue of Selfishness, 44
feedback.note: The passage establishes that sacrifice is the surrender of a greater value for the sake of a lesser one or of a nonvalue. A cost paid to gain a higher value is not that surrender, because the rank runs the other way. Giving up the lesser for the greater is a gain. Rejecting the worthless in favor of the precious is the policy a sacrifice violates, not the definition of one.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition of the act that sacrifice names.

parts.text: A sacrifice surrenders a greater value for a lesser one or for a

feedback.note: Nonvalue completes the definition, because the thing accepted need not be a small value. It can be nothing one values at all. Profit, purpose, and principle are not names for that remainder. They are what a rational exchange is trying to secure. The definition turns on rank, including the case where the second term does not deserve to be called a value.

exercises.prompt: Someone gives up a fraud he was tempted by and keeps his reputation, which he ranks far higher. Is the refusal a sacrifice?

choices.text: Yes, because he gave up something he was tempted to take
Yes, because every refusal feels like a loss
Yes, if a bystander calls the fraud an opportunity
No. He rejected a lesser or empty course for a value he ranks higher

feedback.note: The refusal is not a sacrifice, because he kept the greater value and gave up a temptation that was not higher in his hierarchy. Temptation and a feeling of loss do not set the rank. A bystander's label does not either. Sacrifice would be surrendering the reputation for the fraud. He did the opposite, which is what a hierarchy is for.

exercises.prompt: A nonvalue, in this definition, is which of the following?

choices.text: Something that does not stand as a value in the hierarchy doing the choosing
Any costly effort, including effort that gains a higher value
The greater of the two values
Whatever a crowd is willing to applaud

feedback.note: A nonvalue here is something the chooser does not hold as a value, because the surrender is then of a real value for nothing in his hierarchy. Costly effort toward a higher value is not a nonvalue. The greater value is the thing sacrifice gives up, not the name of what replaces it. Applause does not decide the rank. His values do.

exercises.prompt: Build the definition in the order the ranks require.

feedback.note: Sacrifice surrenders a greater value for a lesser value or a nonvalue. "A higher value" would reverse the ranks, and "every cost" would name payments that buy something one values more, because those payments are not sacrifices. The definition is a claim about rank. It is not a claim that giving anything up is morally special.

exercises.prompt: When is a cost that someone pays not a sacrifice?

choices.text: Never. Every cost surrenders a greater value
When it is paid to gain a value one ranks higher than the cost
When the cost hurts, because hurt is the definition
When one receives nothing one values, and calls the nothing a gain

feedback.note: A cost is not a sacrifice when it buys a higher value, because the exchange moves up one's hierarchy rather than down. Not every cost surrenders the greater value. Hurt is not the definition. Receiving nothing and calling it a gain would be a surrender for a nonvalue, which is a sacrifice. The difference is the rank, not the presence of a price.

exercises.prompt: A student pays tuition for an education he values more than the money. What is the tuition?

choices.text: A cost paid for a higher value, not a sacrifice
A sacrifice, because the money is gone
A sacrifice, because learning takes effort
Neither a cost nor a value, because education is free of rank

feedback.note: The tuition is a cost of a higher value, because he ranks the education above the money. The money's being gone is what a cost is, not what a sacrifice is. Effort does not change the rank. Education is not free of rank. It is the greater value in his judgment, which is why paying is a gain rather than a surrender of something he holds more dear.

exercises.prompt: Match each payment to what the ranks make it.

pairs.left: Money paid for a tool one values more than the money
A career surrendered for a trivial comfort
The alternative one did not choose, in a trade upward

feedback.note: The tool is a higher value, so the money is a cost. The career surrendered for a trivial comfort is a greater value given up, so it is a sacrifice. Every choice forgoes an alternative, and that forgoing is not yet a sacrifice, because the alternative may be the lesser value. If every forgone option were a sacrifice, no rational choice could avoid the name.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about an exchange of a penny for a dollar?
exercises.quote: If you exchange a penny for a dollar, it is not a sacrifice; if you exchange a dollar for a penny, it is.

choices.text: Both exchanges are sacrifices, because both give something up
The penny for the dollar is the sacrifice, because one parts with the penny
The penny for the dollar is not a sacrifice. The dollar for the penny is
Neither is a sacrifice, because money cannot stand in a hierarchy

feedback.quote: If you exchange a penny for a dollar, it is not a sacrifice; if you exchange a dollar for a penny, it is.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 139
feedback.note: The passage establishes the direction. Exchanging a penny for a dollar is not a sacrifice, and exchanging a dollar for a penny is, because the first gains the greater value and the second surrenders it. Parting with something is not enough. Money can stand in a hierarchy. The amounts are a plain case of rank. The same test applies when the values are not coins.

exercises.prompt: Complete the exchange that is not a sacrifice.

parts.text: Exchanging a penny for a dollar is not a

feedback.note: Sacrifice is the word that does not apply, because the dollar outranks the penny and the exchange moves up. Exchange, gain, and trade are names for what the penny-for-dollar case is. Putting them in the blank would call the upward trade a non-exchange or a non-gain, which reverses the point. The downward trade, a dollar for a penny, is the sacrifice.

exercises.prompt: Every choice leaves something unchosen. Why does that fact not make every choice a sacrifice?

choices.text: It does. The unchosen option is always the greater value
It does not, only when the choice is painful
It does not, because choices do not involve values
The unchosen option may be the lesser value. Giving it up is then a cost of a gain

feedback.note: The unchosen option is not automatically the greater value, because a rational choice gives up the lesser for the greater. That giving-up is a cost, not a sacrifice. Pain is not the test, and choices are made of values. If the forgone option outranks the one accepted, then the choice is a sacrifice. The mere fact of forgoing does not settle which way the ranks run.

exercises.prompt: A founder invests his savings in a company he values more than the savings. A critic calls the investment a sacrifice because the savings are at risk. What is the critic using as his test?

choices.text: The founder's ranking, which puts the company first
The presence of a cost and a risk, rather than the rank of the two values
The definition that only a downward trade is a sacrifice
The difference between a penny and a dollar

feedback.note: The critic is using cost and risk as the test, because he does not ask whether the founder values the company more than the savings. The founder's ranking is the test he skipped. The definition that only a downward trade is a sacrifice is the one the critic is not using. Risk does not by itself reverse a hierarchy. A cost paid for a higher value remains a cost.

exercises.prompt: Build the distinction between a cost and a sacrifice.

feedback.note: A cost paid for a higher value is not a sacrifice. "Any loss" would erase the distinction, and a downward trade is what a sacrifice is, because that trade surrenders the greater value. The penny bought for a dollar is the plain upward case. Tuition, tools, and effort follow the same test whenever the person ranks the gain above the payment.

exercises.prompt: Why is the act called sacrifice not a virtue?

choices.text: It surrenders a greater value, so it moves against the life the virtues exist to sustain
Because it hurts, and hurt is what makes an act a vice
Because every loss is evil, including a cost paid for a higher value
Because a rational life requires one to surrender one's highest values

feedback.note: Sacrifice is not a virtue because it gives up what one's life, by one's own hierarchy, holds as greater. The virtues exist to sustain that life, not to undermine it. Hurt is not the test, and a cost paid for a higher value is not evil. A requirement to surrender one's highest values would invert the standard. Human good does not require that inversion, and it cannot be achieved by it.

exercises.prompt: A code praises a woman for dropping the work she lives by in order to serve a cause she ranks as nothing, and it calls the drop her finest act. What has the code praised?

choices.text: A virtue, because the cause was called fine
A cost of a higher value, which is what the drop is
A sacrifice, and the praise treats that sacrifice as a virtue
Justice, because the cause had earned her life

feedback.note: The code has praised a sacrifice, because she surrendered a greater value for a nonvalue, and it has called that surrender her finest act. The label "fine" does not change her ranking. The drop is not a cost of a higher value. Justice did not find that the cause had earned her life. She judged it as nothing. Praising the drop inverts good and evil.

exercises.prompt: Match each ground to what it does, or does not, show.

pairs.left: It surrenders the greater value
pairs.right: Why sacrifice is not a virtue

pairs.left: It hurts
pairs.right: Not the reason, and not the definition

pairs.left: It is a cost of something ranked higher
pairs.right: A reason it is not a sacrifice, and not a vice

feedback.note: The surrender of the greater value is why the act is not a virtue, because the good is what sustains one's life and this act moves against that hierarchy. Hurt is a poor test. It fits some costs and some sacrifices and defines neither. A cost of a higher value is not the act under discussion, so it supplies no duty to praise self-surrender. The code does not need that praise.

exercises.prompt: Complete the moral status that a sacrifice has.

parts.text: Sacrifice is not a

feedback.note: Virtue is the status it does not have, because a virtue is a policy that sustains one's life and a sacrifice surrenders a greater value. Loss, choice, and fact can be true of the act without making it a virtue. The error is the promotion, not the recognition that something was given up. Giving up the greater for the lesser is a real act and a bad one.

exercises.prompt: A man feels pain while paying for a medicine he values more than the money and the pain. A spectator says the pain makes the payment virtuous. What did the spectator need the pain to do?

choices.text: Nothing. Pain is irrelevant, and he did not rely on it
Prove that the medicine outranks the money, which the pain does prove
Show that the man sacrificed a higher value, which he did
Stand in for a virtue, in an act that is a cost of a higher value and not a sacrifice

feedback.note: The spectator needed the pain to do the work of a virtue, because there is no downward trade to praise. The payment is a cost of the medicine, which the man ranks higher. Pain does not prove that rank, and it does not create a sacrifice. Praising him for hurting confuses a cost with a surrender of his life. The virtue, if any is involved, is the rationality of buying what his life requires.

exercises.prompt: Why can human good not be achieved by sacrificing anyone to anyone?

choices.text: Because a sacrifice destroys a greater value, and the good is not built out of that destruction
Because nobody has values, so there is nothing to surrender
Because every cost is forbidden, including a cost paid for a higher value
Because the good requires each person to come out worse

feedback.note: The good cannot be achieved that way because a sacrifice surrenders a greater value for a lesser one or a nonvalue, and a good life is not assembled from those surrenders. People do have values. That is why the surrender is real. Costs of higher values are not forbidden. A requirement to come out worse is the altruist demand, which is the doctrine that treats sacrifice as the ideal. It is not the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Which praise is consistent with the claim that sacrifice is not a virtue?

choices.text: Praise for paying a real cost in order to secure a value one ranks higher
Praise for dropping one's highest value because a lesser claim asked
Praise for surrendering a value to a nonvalue and calling the blank a moral peak
Praise for pain itself, with no question about what was gained

feedback.note: Praise for a cost that secures a higher value is consistent, because that act is not a sacrifice and it serves the life the virtues protect. Praise for a downward trade, for a surrender to a nonvalue, or for pain as such treats sacrifice, or a mere hurt, as the good. Those are the praises the claim rules out. The allowed praise is praise of a gain, not of a loss misdescribed as one.

exercises.prompt: Build the reason sacrifice is not a virtue.

feedback.note: Sacrifice is not a virtue because it surrenders a greater value. "It hurts" is the wrong test, and "every cost is evil" condemns payments that buy higher values, because those payments are not the surrender at issue. The virtues are policies of sustaining one's life. A policy of giving up what that life ranks higher cannot be one of them.

exercises.prompt: What decides whether an exchange is a sacrifice?

choices.text: The rank of the two values in the hierarchy of the person choosing
Whether the exchange is visible to other people
Whether anything at all is given up, regardless of rank
Whether the chooser suffers, regardless of what he gains

feedback.note: Rank decides, because a sacrifice surrenders the greater value for the lesser or for a nonvalue, and only the chooser's hierarchy says which is greater. Visibility, the mere fact of giving something up, and suffering are not the test. A painful cost of a higher value is not a sacrifice. A painless surrender of a higher value is. The feeling is not a substitute for the ranking.

exercises.prompt: A mother buys food for her hungry child rather than a hat for herself, because she values the child more than the hat. Is the purchase a sacrifice?

choices.text: Yes, because she did not get the hat
Yes, because a child is always a duty and never a value
No. She gave up the lesser value for the greater one
Yes, whenever a parent spends money on a child

feedback.note: The purchase is not a sacrifice, because she values the child more than the hat and acts on that rank. The missing hat is the lesser value, a cost of the greater one. The child is not converted into a mere duty by being valued. Spending on a child is not automatically a sacrifice. It is a sacrifice only if she ranks the hat higher and buys the food against that rank, from duty.

exercises.prompt: Match each mother's ranking to the name of her purchase.

pairs.left: She values the child more than the hat and buys the food
She values the hat more, and buys the food only because duty demands it
She values neither, and buys at random
pairs.right: Not a verdict until a rank exists

feedback.note: The first mother acts on her hierarchy, so the food is the greater value and the hat is a cost. The second surrenders what she holds as greater, the hat, for a lesser or a nonvalue in her own ranking, because duty rather than her values selected the food. That is a sacrifice. Without a rank there is nothing to compare, so the word cannot be applied by the size of the grocery bill.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test that the ranking supplies.

parts.text: The exchange is a sacrifice only if the value surrendered ranks
than the value accepted.

feedback.note: Higher completes the test, because sacrifice is the surrender of the greater for the lesser or the nonvalue. Lower would describe a gain, the penny for the dollar. Equal does not name a greater value given up. Nowhere denies the comparison the definition requires. The mother who prefers her child is not in the higher-surrender case. The mother who prefers the hat, and acts from duty, is.

exercises.prompt: The same mother, in a different season, wants the hat more than she wants the child fed, and she buys the food only because she thinks duty requires the surrender. What changed?

choices.text: Nothing. Both purchases are sacrifices because a hat was involved
The food became a nonvalue, so the duty purchase is a gain
The first purchase was the sacrifice, and this one is a trade upward
The rank. This purchase surrenders what she holds as greater, so it is a sacrifice

feedback.note: The rank changed, and with it the name of the act, because sacrifice is not "buying food" or "skipping a hat." It is surrendering the greater value. In this season the hat is what she holds as greater, and duty is asking her to give it up. The first purchase was the upward act. Calling both sacrifices, or calling this one a gain, ignores the only fact that decides the question.

exercises.prompt: A collector sells a sketch he ranks as minor in order to keep a painting he ranks as the center of his work. A friend sells the painting to buy the sketch, and says they did the same thing. Did they?

choices.text: Yes, because each sold a picture
No. One traded up. The other surrendered the greater value for the lesser
Yes, because both felt the loss of the sold picture
No, only because the painting is always a sacrifice to sell

feedback.note: They did not do the same thing, because the ranks run in opposite directions. The first collector paid a lesser value for a greater one. The friend surrendered the center of his work for a minor sketch, which is a sacrifice. The feeling of loss attends both sales and decides neither. The painting is not a sacrifice to sell when what he keeps outranks it. The objects do not carry the rank. The hierarchy does.

exercises.prompt: Why can an outsider not settle the question by announcing that children always outrank hats, or that hats always outrank children?

choices.text: Because the rank that matters is the chooser's hierarchy, not a rank assigned from outside
Because children and hats cannot be values to anyone
Because every purchase is a sacrifice, so the announcement is unnecessary
Because duty, not a hierarchy, is what the word sacrifice ignores

feedback.note: The outsider's announcement does not settle it, because sacrifice is defined by the chooser's ranking, and a mother can value her child above a hat without that value being a duty. Children and hats can both be values. Not every purchase is a sacrifice. Duty is what turns the downward case into a sacrifice when she acts against her own rank. It is not a substitute for finding out what that rank is.

exercises.prompt: Build the test that the ranking of values supplies.

feedback.note: If the value given up ranks higher, the exchange is a sacrifice. "Any cost suffices" and "pain decides" drop the ranking, because a cost of a higher value and a painful gain are not surrenders of what one holds as greater. The mother and the hat are the same test in a personal case. Her values, not the grocery list and not a spectator's duty, settle it.

exercises.prompt: Which statement holds the whole claim about sacrifice?

choices.text: Every loss is a sacrifice, and a sacrifice is a virtue
A sacrifice surrenders a greater value for a lesser or a nonvalue, and that is not a virtue
A cost of a higher value is a sacrifice, but it is the central virtue
Rank is irrelevant, and pain is both the definition and the ideal

feedback.note: The whole claim joins the definition to the moral conclusion, because surrendering a greater value for a lesser one or a nonvalue moves against one's life and is not a virtue. Every loss is too wide. A cost of a higher value is not the act defined. Pain is neither the definition nor the ideal. The mother who feeds a child she values more has not performed the act, and she does not need it praised as one.

exercises.prompt: A guest calls a mother's grocery trip a noble sacrifice, though she values the child more than the hat, and he calls another man noble for quitting the work he ranks first in order to receive empty praise he himself calls worthless. What should be separated?

choices.text: The trip is not a sacrifice. The quitting is a sacrifice, and it is not a virtue
Both are noble sacrifices, because both gave something up
The trip is the sacrifice, and the quitting is a cost of a higher value
Neither involves a rank, so both are virtues by being visible

feedback.note: The trip is not a sacrifice, because the child outranks the hat, and the quitting is a sacrifice, because the work outranks praise he counts as nothing. Nobility does not glue them together. Giving something up is not the definition. The quitting is not a cost of a higher value. It is the downward trade, and praising it treats a sacrifice as a virtue. The two acts need two judgments.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to the full judgment it deserves.

pairs.left: Food bought because the child outranks the hat
pairs.right: A cost of a higher value, not a sacrifice

pairs.left: A career quit for praise one does not value
pairs.right: A sacrifice, and not a virtue

pairs.left: A dollar exchanged for a penny
A penny exchanged for a dollar
pairs.right: Not a sacrifice, and not a virtue by being one

feedback.note: The food is a cost of the greater value. The career quit for worthless praise surrenders a greater value for a nonvalue, so it is a sacrifice and not a virtue. The dollar for the penny is the same downward rank in numbers. The penny for the dollar is a gain, and it does not become a virtue by being miscalled a sacrifice. The whole claim uses one test and then refuses to praise the act that fails it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two halves of the claim about sacrifice.

parts.text: A sacrifice surrenders a greater value, and it is not a

feedback.note: Virtue is the status the second half denies, because the act moves against the life a virtue would sustain. Cost, rank, and choice are involved in deciding whether an act is a sacrifice at all. They do not name what the act is being refused as. The first half is the definition. The second half is why the definition is not a compliment.

exercises.prompt: A speaker proves that an act was costly, painful, and admired, and he concludes that it was a virtuous sacrifice. What has he not yet shown?

choices.text: That anyone noticed it, which is all the definition requires
That it hurt, which is the definition he still needs
That it was admired, which fixes the rank
That a greater value was surrendered for a lesser one or a nonvalue

feedback.note: He has not shown the rank, because cost, pain, and admiration do not establish that the greater value was given up. Notice is not the definition. Hurt is not the definition. Admiration does not fix the chooser's hierarchy. Until the ranks are known, he cannot call it a sacrifice, and even then the further conclusion that it was a virtue does not follow. Both halves of the claim are still open.

exercises.prompt: Which policy is the one a person should follow, given the whole claim?

choices.text: Surrender the greater value whenever a lesser one, or a duty, asks
Call every cost a sacrifice, and seek such costs as the good
Act by the hierarchy of one's values, and do not surrender a greater value to a lesser
Refuse every cost, including a cost that buys a value one ranks higher

feedback.note: The policy is to act by one's hierarchy and not surrender the greater to the lesser, because that is the alternative to sacrifice and the reason sacrifice is not a virtue. A standing surrender is the act itself. Collecting costs as if they were the good repeats the error that every loss qualifies. Refusing a cost that buys a higher value refuses gains, not sacrifices. The mother who values her child buys the food. She does not need a theory that calls the purchase noble self-destruction.

exercises.prompt: A final case looks mixed: he pays a real fee to keep a contract he ranks above the fee, and he also drops a friendship he ranks above the contract in order to impress a stranger he does not respect. What are the two parts?

choices.text: Both parts are sacrifices, and both are virtues
The fee is a cost of a higher value. Dropping the friendship is a sacrifice and not a virtue
The fee is the sacrifice. The friendship is a nonvalue he was right to scorn
Neither part can be judged, because a fee and a friendship are both invisible

feedback.note: The fee buys the contract he ranks higher, so it is a cost. Dropping the friendship surrenders a greater value for the regard of someone he does not respect, which is a lesser value or a nonvalue, so it is a sacrifice and not a virtue. The mixture does not make the fee into self-destruction or the friendship into nothing. Each part has its own rank. The whole claim is the habit of splitting them.

exercises.prompt: Build the whole claim about what a sacrifice is.

feedback.note: Sacrifice surrenders a greater value and is not a virtue. "Every loss" is too wide, and "a noble cost" praises the wrong act, because a cost of a higher value is not the surrender and does not need to be called one in order to be rational. Rank decides the name. The name, once earned, is not a term of praise.
